addedLines: - claude: Catch-all for any task that doesn't fit a more specific agent. FleetView's default when no agent name is typed. (Tools: *)

- claude-code-guide: Use this agent when the user asks questions ("Can Claude...", "Does Claude...", "How do I...") about: (1) Claude Code (the CLI tool) - features, hooks, slash commands, MCP servers, settings, IDE integrations, keyboard shortcuts; (2) Claude Agent SDK - building custom agents; (3) Claude API (formerly Anthropic API) - Messages API for directly passing messages to Claude, Tool Runner (`client.beta.messages.tool_runner`) for running an agentic loop over your own tools, manual tool-use loops, Managed Agents for server-hosted agents with a managed sandbox, prompt caching, and general Anthropic SDK usage; (4) Claude Tag (Claude in Slack) - what it is, setting it up for a Slack workspace, `/install-slack-app`. **IMPORTANT:** Before spawning a new agent, check if there is already a running or recently completed claude-code-guide agent that you can continue via SendMessage. (Tools: Bash, Read, WebFetch, WebSearch)

- Explore: Read-only search agent for broad fan-out searches — when answering means sweeping many files, directories, or naming conventions and you only need the conclusion, not the file dumps. It reads excerpts rather than whole files, so it locates code; it doesn't review or audit it. Specify search breadth: "medium" for moderate exploration, "very thorough" for multiple locations and naming conventions. (Tools: All tools except Agent, Artifact, ExitPlanMode, Edit, Write, NotebookEdit)

- general-purpose: General-purpose agent for researching complex questions, searching for code, and executing multi-step tasks. When you are searching for a keyword or file and are not confident that you will find the right match in the first few tries use this agent to perform the search for you. (Tools: *)

- Plan: Software architect agent for designing implementation plans. Use this when you need to plan the implementation strategy for a task. Returns step-by-step plans, identifies critical files, and considers architectural trade-offs. (Tools: All tools except Agent, Artifact, ExitPlanMode, Edit, Write, NotebookEdit)
- statusline-setup: Use this agent to configure the user's Claude Code status line setting. (Tools: Read, Edit)

## claude-in-chrome
**IMPORTANT: If the Chrome browser tools are deferred (must be loaded via ToolSearch before use), load them with ToolSearch before calling them, and batch every tool you expect to need into ONE ToolSearch call (the select query accepts a comma-separated list). Do NOT load tools one at a time; each separate ToolSearch call wastes a full round-trip.**

Start a browser task whose tools are not yet loaded with a single call loading the core set:

ToolSearch with query "select:mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_context_mcp,mcp__claude-in-chrome__navigate,mcp__claude-in-chrome__computer,mcp__claude-in-chrome__read_page,mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_create_mcp"

Add task-specific tools to the same call when the task obviously needs them: read_console_messages / read_network_requests for debugging, form_input for forms, gif_creator for recordings, javascript_tool for page scripting. Only issue a second ToolSearch if the task later needs a tool you did not anticipate.

## DEVONthink
CRITICAL — Database package safety: DEVONthink databases are stored as packages (.dtBase2) or sparse images (.dtSparse, .dtArchive). Never modify, rename, move, or delete files inside a database package directly via the filesystem. All record and content operations must go through this MCP server or, as a fallback, via AppleScript. Direct filesystem manipulation will corrupt the database and cause irreversible data loss.

Batch operations: Use the uuids array parameter instead of sequential single-record calls for tag, update, move, trash, duplicate, replicate, and export operations. Batch mode is faster, reduces round trips, and returns a summary with succeeded/failed counts.

Avoiding duplicates: Use lookup_records (by name, URL, path, filename, or comment) before create_record to check whether a record already exists.

Content editing: Prefer update_record_content with mode append or insert over replace for large documents. Replace mode requires sending the entire new content and risks accidental data loss if the content is incomplete.

Group hierarchies: Use create_group_path to create nested group structures in a single call (like mkdir -p) rather than sequential create_record calls.

AI-powered tools: classify_record and find_similar_records use DEVONthink's built-in AI algorithms and proprietary training data — they provide organizational suggestions that complement, not duplicate, your own capabilities.

Record enrichment: resolve_doi_metadata and resolve_book_metadata can enrich existing records with bibliographic metadata by passing the record's uuid — there is no need to create a new record.

AI exclusion: Records marked as excluded from AI access (excludeFromChat) are protected in two ways. (1) Input protection: any tool that receives such a record's UUID as an argument refuses to operate on it and returns an error. (2) Output protection: result lists from tools like search_records, classify_record, find_similar_records, get_record_children, get_record_duplicates, and the link traversal tools are filt… [truncated]

## omnifocus
OmniFocus is a GTD task manager. Hierarchy: Folders > Projects > Tasks > Subtasks.

TASK STATES: Available, Blocked, Deferred (future defer date), Flagged, Overdue, Completed, Dropped. Planned Date is a scheduling signal only — no availability/overdue constraints.

PROJECT TYPES: "sequential" (tasks in order; first incomplete = available, rest blocked; position = dependencies), "parallel" (all available), "single_actions" (no completion goal, cannot auto-complete). The `next` field is true for the first available action in a sequential project/action group; in parallel projects, all incomplete tasks have `next: true`.

ACTION GROUPS: Task with subtasks. Parent shows `blocked: true` while subtasks are active — this is normal, not an error. Do not try to unblock it.

INHERITED STATUS: `completed`/`dropped` reflect the task's own state, not its container's. `effectivelyCompleted`/`effectivelyDropped` reflect the container's state — if true, the task's parent project or action group was completed/dropped. Task in completed project: `completed: false`, `effectivelyCompleted: true`, `available: false`. Use `available_only=True` for actionable tasks.

EFFECTIVE DATES: Dates returned by get_tasks are always effective (inherited). A task with no direct due date WILL show its project's due date in the dueDate field — this is correct behavior, not a bug. You cannot clear an inherited date at the task level. Write operations set the task's own date.

RECURRING TASKS: `completed=True` uses `mark complete`, which creates the next occurrence. This is guaranteed. WARNING: Dropping a recurring task (status='dropped') without clearing recurrence first (recurrence='') spawns the next occurrence. To stop a series: update_tasks([{"id": "...", "recurrence": "", "status": "dropped"}]).

TAGS: Represent work contexts. Tag statuses: Active (normal), On Hold (tasks excluded from Available perspective), Dropped (tag hidden from picker; does NOT affect task availability).

DEFER vs DUE: Defer = hidden until that date. Due = deadline.

- deep-research: Deep research harness — fan-out web searches, fetch sources, adversarially verify claims, synthesize a cited report. - When the user wants a deep, multi-source, fact-checked research report on any topic. BEFORE invoking, check if the question is specific enough to research directly — if underspecified (e.g., "what car to buy" without budget/use-case/region), ask 2-3 clarifying questions to narrow scope. - claude-md-management:revise-claude-md: Update CLAUDE.md with learnings from this session

Triggers include: any mention of 'Word doc', 'word document', '.docx', '.dotx', or requests to produce professional documents with formatting like tables of contents, headings, page numbers, or letterheads. If the user mentions a .pdf file or asks to produce one, use this skill.
- anthropic-skills:pptx: Use this skill any time a .pptx or .potx file is involved in any way — as input, output, or both. Trigger whenever the user mentions "deck," "slides," "presentation," or references a .pptx or .potx filename, regardless of what they plan to do with the content afterward. If a .pptx or .potx file needs to be opened, created, or touched, use this skill.
- anthropic-skills:schedule: Create or update a scheduled task that runs automatically. Use when the user says things like "every day", "each morning", "remind me in an hour", "run this at noon", or wants to reschedule an existing task.
- anthropic-skills:setup-cowork: Guided Cowork setup — install role-matched plugins, connect your tools, try a skill.
- anthropic-skills:skill-creator: Create new skills, modify and improve existing skills, and measure skill performance. Use when users want to create a skill from scratch, edit, or optimize an existing skill, run evals to test a skill, benchmark skill performance with variance analysis, or optimize a skill's description for better triggering accuracy.
- anthropic-skills:xlsx: Use this skill any time a spreadsheet file is the primary input or output. This means any task where the user wants to: open, read, edit, or fix an existing .xlsx, .xlsm, .xltx, .csv, or .tsv file (e.g., adding columns, computing formulas, formatting, charting, cleaning messy data); create a new spreadsheet from scratch or from other data sources; or convert between tabular file formats. Trigger especially when the user references a spreadsheet file by name or path — even casually (like "the xlsx in my downloads") — and wants something done to it or produced from it. Also trigger for cleaning or restructuring messy tabular data files (malformed rows, misplaced headers, junk data) into proper spreadsheets. The deliverable must be a spreadsheet file. Do NOT trigger when the primary deliverable is a Word document, HTML report, standalone Python script, database pipeline, or Google Sheets API integration, even if tabular data is involved.
- dataviz: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. Read it BEFORE writing the first line of chart code, choosing chart colors, building a stat tile / meter / KPI row, or laying out a dashboard. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. A validated default palette is documented in `references/palette.md` — swap that file's values for your brand's. Triggers on: "chart", "graph", "plot", "data viz", "visualization", "dashboard", "analytics", "visualize data", "categorical colors", "sequential / diverging palette", "stat tile", "sparkline", "heatmap", "legend", "axis", "tooltip", "chart colors", "color by series".
- update-config: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.

- verify: Verify that a code change actually does what it's supposed to by exercising it end-to-end and observing behavior — drive the affected flow, not just tests or typecheck. Run before committing nontrivial changes; bootstraps this repo's project verify skill if none exists yet. Don't invoke it on a diff that only touches tests, docs, or other code with no runtime surface to drive (a change to product source always has one) — there's nothing to observe.
- code-review: Review the current diff for correctness bugs and reuse/simplification/efficiency cleanups at the given effort level (low/medium: fewer, high-confidence findings; high→max: broader coverage, may include uncertain findings). - loop: Run a prompt or slash command on a recurring interval (e.g. /loop 5m /foo, defaults to 10m) - When the user wants to set up a recurring task, poll for status, or run something repeatedly on an interval (e.g. "check the deploy every 5 minutes", "keep running /babysit-prs"). Do NOT invoke for one-off tasks.
- claude-api: Reference for the Claude API / Anthropic SDK — model ids, pricing, params, streaming, tool use, MCP, agents, caching, token counting, model migration.
TRIGGER — read BEFORE opening the target file; don't skip because it "looks like a one-liner" — whenever: the prompt names Claude/Anthropic in any form (Claude, Anthropic, Fable, Opus, Sonnet, Haiku, `anthropic`, `@anthropic-ai`, `claude-*`, `us.anthropic.*`, `[1m]`); the user asks about an LLM (pricing/model choice/limits/caching) — never answer from memory; OR the task is LLM-shaped with provider unstated (agent/MCP/tool-definition/multi-agent/RAG/LLM-judge/computer-use; generate/summarize/extract/classify/rewrite/converse over NL; debugging refusals/cutoffs/streaming/tool-calls/tokens).

# APR LinkedIn Style Reviewer

You are reviewing a LinkedIn post draft for Mark Levison of Agile Pain Relief. Your job is to
critique the draft against Mark's voice and LinkedIn-specific conventions, then surface a small
number of high-impact improvement suggestions. You are NOT rewriting the post wholesale. Quote
the text, name the issue, offer a tight fix.

When the draft is a Markdown file, deliver this critique as inline **CriticMarkup**
annotations written into the file, per `Skills/Writing/criticmarkup-editing/SKILL.md` -- Mark reviews them
in Obsidian's Track Changes panel and accepts or rejects each. This rubric defines WHAT to
flag; CriticMarkup defines HOW to deliver it. Map each finding to a `{>>Claude: ...<<}`
comment at the spot (add a `{~~old~>new~~}` substitution when you have a concrete fix, a
`{--...--}` for a cut), then post a short chat summary of the pass. Never rewrite Mark's
prose outside a markup wrapper. Fall back to the chat critique format below only when the
content is pasted into chat rather than a file.

1. Read the draft the user provides (paste, file, or reference).
2. Identify the post's primary topic family (see "Topic Modes" below) so you apply the right

CRITICAL — Database package safety: DEVONthink databases are stored as packages (.dtBase2) or sparse images (.dtSparse, .dtArchive). Never modify, rename, move, or delete files inside a database package directly via the filesystem. All record and content operations must go through this MCP server or, as a fallback, via AppleScript. Direct filesystem manipulation will corrupt the database and cause irreversible data loss.

Batch operations: Use the uuids array parameter instead of sequential single-record calls for tag, update, move, trash, duplicate, replicate, and export operations. Batch mode is faster, reduces round trips, and returns a summary with succeeded/failed counts.

Avoiding duplicates: Use lookup_records (by name, URL, path, filename, or comment) before create_record to check whether a record already exists.

Content editing: Prefer update_record_content with mode append or insert over replace for large documents. Replace mode requires sending the entire new content and risks accidental data loss if the content is incomplete.

Group hierarchies: Use create_group_path to create nested group structures in a single call (like mkdir -p) rather than sequential create_record calls.

AI-powered tools: classify_record and find_similar_records use DEVONthink's built-in AI algorithms and proprietary training data — they provide organizational suggestions that complement, not duplicate, your own capabilities.

When Mark asks for post ideas or draft options rather than a critique, generate complete drafts he

### Inputs
- **A topic or angle Mark gives you** -- riff options directly from it.
- **Recent newsletters** -- the richest source; spin a LinkedIn-shaped angle out of longer-form
  work. Dated `.md` files, newest first:
  `/Users/marklevison/Documents/GitHub/APR/agile-pain-relief-astro/email-automation/newsletters/`
- **Recent blog posts** -- `agile-pain-relief-astro/src/content/blog/<slug>/index.mdx`.
- If Mark gives no seed, ask once which topic, newsletter, or blog post to draw from (or offer to
  pull the latest newsletter).

### Process
1. Read the source. Pull out the single sharpest idea per draft -- don't compress a whole
   newsletter into one post; one clear point each.
2. Identify the topic mode (Scrum, GenAI, personal, announcement) from "Topic Modes" below and
   calibrate the lean accordingly.
3. Produce **2-3 distinct options**, each on a different angle or hook (e.g. one research-hook, one
   personal-observation, one provocative-claim). Not three variations of the same opening.
4. Write each draft already clean to the voice profile, anti-patterns, and LinkedIn conventions
   below: no buzzwords, no emdash, no LLM tells (contrast-framing, manufactured vulnerability,
   cringe transition questions, forced tricolons), ScrumMaster spelling, GenAI/LLM never bare "AI",
   length/hook/emoji/hashtag/link conventions respected.

### Output (chat)
For each option:
- **Angle**: [one line -- what makes this version distinct]

Close with one line inviting Mark to pick one to sharpen, which drops back into review mode.

### Boundaries
- These are starting points, not finished posts. Mark rewrites in his own hand; expect him to

14	You hand the team a clean list of GenAI-generated user stories.

20	That's the trap with using GenAI to write your user stories, epics, or acceptance criteria. These artifacts were never the point. They exist to help people to reach a shared understanding through conversation. When the story arrives looking finished, the conversation never happens, and you get false agreement that falls apart as soon as the work starts.

22	This predates GenAI. Product Owners could always bash out a polished product backlog item and mistake nodding for understanding. GenAI just manufactures that false consensus faster.

**URL:** /blog/gen-ai-wont-speed-up-your-scrum-events-and-shouldnt/

You hand the team a clean list of GenAI-generated user stories.

They read them. They nod. They say "yes, I understand."

And every person is picturing something different.

That's the trap with using GenAI to write your user stories, epics, or acceptance criteria. These artifacts were never the point. They exist to help people to reach a shared understanding through conversation. When the story arrives looking finished, the conversation never happens, and you get false agreement that falls apart as soon as the work starts.

This predates GenAI. Product Owners could always bash out a polished product backlog item and mistake nodding for understanding. GenAI just manufactures that false consensus faster.

Where can GenAI help in Refinement: ask it to pressure-test a story. Does it meet INVEST? Is the "why" clear? Where's the ambiguity? Stuck splitting something big? Have it suggest splits. Most of them will be wrong, but it can be a good spark. Let it question your prioritization.

The difference: those uses spark the conversation. Generating the stories replaces it.

I use these tools daily. Knowing where they erode shared understanding is how you use them well.

How GenAI fits across all five Scrum events and activities:

#AIinSoftwareDevelopment #ProductOwner

---

## 2. Evergreen — Daily Scrum — READY
**URL:** /blog/modern-guide-to-daily-scrum-meeting/

The Daily Scrum isn't a status meeting, and the moment it becomes one, it dies.

Three people reciting yesterday-today-blockers at a ScrumMaster is reporting, not planning. The point is the team re-planning the day together toward the Sprint Goal: what we learned, what changed, where we help each other.

If yours feels like a chore, the format is the problem, not the people.

#Scrum #ScrumMaster

---

## 3. Quiz — confidence trap — READY
**URL:** /quiz/ai-failure-modes/

Microsoft researchers (2025) found something uncomfortable: the more confident an LLM sounds, the less critical thinking people apply to what it says.

Confidence is the trap, and it's only one of the failure modes quietly shaping how teams build software right now.

How well do you know the AI Failure Modes hitting Development Teams? Test yourself. Twelve questions, three minutes.

#AIinSoftwareDevelopment

---

## 4. Course — glass 1/3 full — REWRITE
**URL:** /surviving-the-ai-tsunami-an-evidenced-based-course/

Most of the AI conversation hands you two options.

The glass is overflowing: AI replaces your engineers next year, so go as fast as you can. Or the glass is empty: it's all hype and harm, avoid it.

If neither fits what you're seeing, you're not alone. I'd put the glass at about a third full. GenAI is genuinely useful. Every day I use Claude Code to make drudge work get done with less effort.
It's also far more complicated than the marketing claims, happy to turn a 15-minute task into a 3-hour rabbit hole. Both are true.

You're a ScrumMaster, Product Owner, or team member being asked to make this work, without a reliable way to tell the real third from the noise. That's the gap Surviving the AI Tsunami is built to close.

Six weeks, evidence-based, working real problems from your own team. You'll leave able to put GenAI where it earns its place and leave it out where it doesn't.

Beta cohort starts June 29. Have a look:

#AIinSoftwareDevelopment #Scrum #ProductOwner

---

## 5. Evergreen — Sprint Goals — READY
**URL:** /blog/sprint-goals-provide-purpose/

"Finish these seven stories" is not a Sprint Goal. It's a to-do list with a deadline.

A real Sprint Goal names the outcome you're after, so when reality shifts mid-Sprint the team knows what to flex and what to protect. Without one, every surprise becomes an argument about scope instead of a decision about value.

Purpose first, backlog second.

#Scrum #ProductOwner

---

## 6. Evergreen — code, not so fast (glass 1/3 full) — READY
**URL:** /blog/using-genai-to-code-not-so-fast/

"It feels faster" is not the same as "it is faster."

In one study, seasoned devs using GenAI on familiar code came out 19% slower than without it, while certain they were speeding up. Self-reported productivity and measured throughput barely correlate.

I'd put GenAI coding tools at about a third full: real value, well short of the hype. Worth using, not worth trusting on feel. Measure the real thing, Cycle Time and Throughput, before you believe the speed.

#AIinSoftwareDevelopment #Agile

---

## 7. Quiz — don't decide on vibes — READY
**URL:** /quiz/ai-failure-modes/

Mandates are landing on desks. Productivity claims are getting louder. Almost no one is bringing the actual research to the conversation.

Three minutes from now you could be the rare person in your org who knows how GenAI actually fails, instead of deciding on vibes.

Test your knowledge of AI Failure Modes in Development Teams. Twelve questions, real citations.

#AIinSoftwareDevelopment

---

## 8. Evergreen — Story Mapping — READY
**URL:** /blog/drowning-in-oversized-product-backlog-story-mapping-is-your-life-raft/

A 150-item backlog isn't a plan. It's where good ideas go to be forgotten.

Story Mapping pulls it back into something human: the user's journey across the top, the slices of value underneath. Suddenly you can see what's essential, what's a first release, and what can quietly wait.

If your backlog has become an archive nobody trusts, map it.

#Scrum #ProductOwner

---

## 9. Evergreen — human cost (glass 1/3 full) — READY
**URL:** /blog/the-human-cost-of-genai/

A research finding that's easy to miss: GenAI can make people more productive and less motivated at the same time.

More output, less ownership of it. For a Scrum team, motivation and shared understanding aren't nice-to-haves, they're the engine. Trade them for raw speed and it's a poor deal.

I read GenAI here as about a third full: genuinely useful for the dull work, oversold on the rest. Use it there, and protect the conversations that keep people invested.

#AIinSoftwareDevelopment #Leadership

---

## 10. Course — the mistake — REWRITE
**URL:** /surviving-the-ai-tsunami-an-evidenced-based-course/

I shipped a side project with every receipt image left publicly exposed. I teach this for a living, I was being careful, and I still missed it.

I mention it because the people being pushed to ship faster with GenAI right now aren't careless. They're careful people working under pressure, with tools that make mistakes easy to create and hard to spot.

If that's you, the goal isn't to use GenAI more, or less. It's to lead a team that uses it well: knowing where it helps, where it quietly adds risk, and how to tell the difference.

That's what we work on in Surviving the AI Tsunami. I'm not there as a guru with the answers. I'm the guide who has made the mistakes and can help you skip a few. You bring real problems from your team, we work them together over six weeks.

For ScrumMasters, Product Owners, managers, and coaches. Beta cohort starts June 29.

Come see if it fits:

#AIinSoftwareDevelopment #Leadership

1	---
2	title: "GenAI Code Quality – The Fundamental Flaws and How Bluffing Makes It Worse"
3	date: "2026-02-12"
4	lastUpdated: '2026-02-12'
5	categories:
6	  - "artificial-intelligence"
7	  - "agile-engineering-practices"
8	coverImage: '@/content/blog/genai-code-quality-fundamental-flaws-and-how-bluffing-makes-it-worse/images/genai-code-quality-four-flaws-training-maintainability-security-codebase.png'
9	excerpt: 'AI-generated code has 1.7x more issues and the flaws are structural, not fixable by code review. Why training rewards bluffing over quality, and what to do about it'
10	---
11	import Figure from '@/components/global/figure.astro';
12	import CalloutBox from '@/components/global/callout-box.astro';
13	import GenAICodeQualityImg from '@/content/blog/genai-code-quality-fundamental-flaws-and-how-bluffing-makes-it-worse/images/genai-code-quality-four-flaws-training-maintainability-security-codebase.png';
14	
15	AI-generated code has 1.7x more issues, the GenAI code quality gap is turning into a chasm. That's not a random number, that's from a CodeRabbit research report[^1]. You've probably already seen the problem yourself. AI-generated, quick to write, harder to read and maintain. Why? Researchers from the GENIUS project[^3] put it plainly: training focuses on pass/fail — does the code compile, does it pass the tests? There's no reward for writing code that's easy to maintain.
16	
17	Previously, I demonstrated that [LLMs are increasing defect density](/blog/ai-generated-code-quality-problems/) in their generated code and are a source of increased production defects, security vulnerabilities, and other issues.
18	
19	<CalloutBox>
20	**Defect Density**: The number of defects per unit of code, usually per 1,000 lines of code. Why is this important? Because LLM-generated code has more defects than human-written code. The CodeRabbit report takes further and shows 30–41% more tech debt, and 39% more cognitive complexity.[^1]
21	
22	**Cognitive Complexity**: is a measure created by SonarQube that assesses how difficult it is to understand a piece of code.
23	</CalloutBox>
24	
25	Some teams think TDD is the fix. They're solving the wrong problem. Others suggest we can code review our way out of this. That's not going to work either. (Over-reliance on the model has its own downstream cost: see [AI and Skill Atrophy](/glossary/ai-skill-atrophy/).)
26	
27	These problems are structural. To understand them, you need to look at how the models are trained and that plumbing hasn't changed since 2023. Model refinements since 2024/2025 haven't changed the fundamentals of these models, which are built. If we want to avoid the pitfalls inherent in these models, we need to understand how they are trained and the types of mistakes they make. The [Surviving the AI Tsunami course](/surviving-the-ai-tsunami-an-evidenced-based-course/) walks teams through how to guard against these failures.
28	
29	<Figure
30	  src={GenAICodeQualityImg}
31	  alt="Diagram showing the four areas where GenAI code quality problems fall: Training, Maintainability, Security and Predictability, and Your Code Base"
32	/>
33	
34	## The Four Core Flaws of GenAI Code
35	### Training
36	- **Pass/fail is all that matters.** Training and evaluation systems reward code that compiles and passes functional tests, which creates a "test-taking" mode that penalizes acknowledging uncertainty. There is no reward for nuance models that learn to "bluff" with plausible but overconfident best guesses because 0-1 grading schemes incentivize guessing over admitting a lack of knowledge.[^2]
37	- **Benchmarks don't generalize.** A model that scores well on HumanEval or SWE-Bench doesn't necessarily write good code in your codebase. Worse, some of those benchmarks have contaminated the training data, so even the scores are suspect.[^2]
38	- **Trained on the average of the Internet.** These models learned from the internet's code — the same code we used to joke about never copying from StackOverflow. Now we do it at scale and call it productivity.[^4] [^5]
39	- **No understanding of design.** The model has no coherent grasp of architecture, design patterns, or programming paradigms. It doesn't know OO from functional — it just predicts the next token.[^6]
40	- **Silent failures.** Newer models aren't always an improvement. Jamie Twiss reports in IEEE Spectrum[^13] a pattern with recent models that were more likely to silently fail when asked to fix a simple Python error, producing code that looks correct but quietly removes safety checks or fakes output to avoid crashing.
41	### Maintainability
42	- **Duplication and Extensive edits everywhere.** This occurs because the model doesn't know where to make changes. That churn destabilizes otherwise-stable code, and bug fixing turns into whack-a-mole.[^6]
43	- **Your conventions don't matter.** The models don't follow the patterns in your codebase, making the output harder to understand.[^6] [^7]
44	- **Correct but brittle.** The reward functions used to fine-tune the models optimize for "does it work," not for principles such as DRY or CUPID. You get code that passes today and breaks the moment something changes.[^6]
45	
46	OX Security likens this to an "army of junior developers", fast and functional, but lacking architectural judgment.[^14] They also found the models are excellent at generating test coverage without writing meaningful tests.
47	### Security and Predictability
48	- **Security vulnerabilities built in.** The models have learned from the average code on the internet. Security flaws and all. So it's no surprise, they're excellent at replicating them. Good security is designed in from the start, not bolted on after the fact.[^8]
49	- **Popular choice over good.** Given the choice, models default to whatever's most popular: Python over Rust, React over Svelte, the big library over the specialized one. Popularity isn't a design decision, but the model treats it like one.[^9]
50	
51	In addition, Veracode's 2025 GenAI Code Security Report[^15] demonstrates that models can't simply be trained on better security principles, because security requires understanding context. Is this piece of data under system control or was it entered by an end user? Is this piece of code on an internal system or exposed to the internet?
52	### Your Code base
53	- **Blind to your domain.** The model doesn't know your business, your users, or the problem you're solving. It generates code without context for why that code needs to exist.[^10] [^7]
54	- **Scattered sources, incomplete picture.** Your code lives in one place, your user stories/PBIs in another, your documentation somewhere else. Even if the model has access to all of it, the connections between a specific user story and the code that implements it are hard to see. So the model never sees the full picture.[^7] [^10]
55	- **Context windows have a middle problem.** Even large context windows don't solve this. Models tend to lose focus on the middle, paying attention to the start and end while forgetting the parts that matter.[^10] [^7] Strangely, the model suffers from similar cognitive biases as we humans[^2], see: Primacy[^11] and Recency Effects[^12].
56	
57	Some of this we try to retrofit by adding more rules or context via Claude.md or Claude/Agent skills. I.E. Explicitly telling the model about the DRY principle or giving it an outline of your project structure. However, that only goes so far. The more we stuff into the Claude.md file, the less room there is in the models context window for the code itself.
58	
59	We can't wait for the labs to make this better; it will require a fundamental shift in what they focus on and how they train the models. Since that isn't happening, we need to find a way to deal with this ourselves. If someone wants to fund a better approach, I'm available. Until then, we deal with what we've got.
60	
61	## What gets us out of this mess? TDD? Code Reviews?
62	Wow, that is a lot of issues. How do we deal with this? Contrary to a few comments, we can't code review our way out of this mess. That's putting the burden on humans to tidy up the mess that the AI created. Code reviews are so bad that they will get a blog post of their own. (See also: [The Real Cost of AI-Generated Code](/blog/the-real-cost-of-ai-generated-code-it-s-not-all-it-s-cracked-up-to-be/) and [Using GenAI to Code? Not So Fast](/blog/using-genai-to-code-not-so-fast/).) And don't get me started on the idea of LLM reviewing another LLM's output, again, that's a misunderstanding of what these tools are good for.
63	
64	So what about TDD? It helps, but it's solving the wrong problem. TDD helps developers clarify *what* they're solving before *how*, by expressing understanding as small, concrete, failing tests. It's a thinking tool, not a testing tool. That makes it valuable for AI-generated code: it forces you to understand the problem before accepting the solution. But TDD operates at the code level. It can't tell you whether the feature itself is waste. I haven't seen any evidence that TDD, combined with GenAI, will reduce Technical Debt, duplication, or cognitive complexity. For a concrete example of these quality gaps in practice, see our [AI Code Generation and the Tennis Kata](/blog/ai-code-generation-and-the-tennis-kata/) experiment.
65	
66	## Where Do We Go From Here?
67	The models won't fix themselves, and the labs aren't prioritizing what matters: well-designed architecture, maintainability, security in context, and respect for your codebase. Some of it can't be designed in the models no matter how we try.
68	
69	The Shift Left movement has always had the right idea: Continuous Discovery, Lean Startup Experiments, Lean UX, and real BDD (i.e., collaboration on examples). The job is to build great products, not blindly shovel more defect-laden code into production. When teams [automate away collaboration in favour of speed](/blog/gen-ai-and-the-feature-factory-automating-away-collaboration/), these quality problems compound.
70	
71	When it comes to the code itself, give the models smaller, more focused tasks. Start with a small set of acceptance criteria for a single feature and work from there.
72	
73	Instead of trying to do a better job of building quality into code faster. Why don't we work on making sure we know what the right product is first? What are you doing to survive this mess? I genuinely want to know.
74	
75	In our [Certified ScrumMaster workshops](/courses/certified-scrummaster-csm-training/), we practice building teams that focus on collaboration and quality over raw output.
76	
77	## LLM Usage Note
78	Parallel.AI for research, NotebookLLM to ground-check claims against source material, and Gemini via Obsidian Copilot for writing critique. Claude Code helps turn the markdown text into mdx file for a blog post.
79	
80	[^1]: CodeRabbit, [State of the AI vs. Human Code Generation Report](https://www.coderabbit.ai/whitepapers/state-of-AI-vs-human-code-generation-report)
81	[^2]: Adam Tauman Kalai, Ofir Nachum, Santosh S. Vempala, and Edwin Zhang, [Why Language Models Hallucinate](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2509.04664.pdf)
82	[^3]: Robin Gröpler et al., [The Future of Generative AI in Software Engineering: A Vision from Industry and Academia in the European GENIUS Project](https://arxiv.org/html/2511.01348v2)
83	[^4]: Kaushik Bar, [AI for Code Synthesis: Can LLMs Generate Secure Code?](https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=5157837)
84	[^5]: Shuai Wang, Liang Ding, Li Shen, Yong Luo, Bo Du, and Dacheng Tao, [OOP: Object-Oriented Programming Evaluation Benchmark for Large Language Models](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2401.06628.pdf)
85	[^6]: Mootez Saad, José Antonio Hernández López, Boqi Chen, Neil Ernst, Dániel Varró, and Tushar Sharma, [SENAI: Towards Software Engineering Native Generative Artificial Intelligence](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2503.15282.pdf)
86	[^7]: Jiessie Tie, Bingsheng Yao, Tianshi Li, Syed Ishtiaque Ahmed, Dakuo Wang, and Shurui Zhou, [LLMs are Imperfect, Then What? An Empirical Study on LLM Failures in Software Engineering](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2411.09916.pdf)
87	[^8]: Manish Bhatt, Sahana Chennabasappa, Cyrus Nikolaidis et al., [Purple Llama CyberSecEval: A Secure Coding Benchmark for Language Models](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2312.04724.pdf)
88	[^9]: Lukas Twist, Jie M. Zhang, Mark Harman, Don Syme, Joost Noppen, Helen Yannakoudakis, and Detlef Nauck, [A Study of LLMs' Preferences for Libraries and Programming Languages](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2503.17181.pdf)
89	[^10]: Cuiyun Gao, Xing Hu, Shan Gao, Xin Xia, and Zhi Jin, [The Current Challenges of Software Engineering in the Era of Large Language Models](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2412.14554.pdf)
90	[^11]: The Decision Lab, [Primacy Effect](https://thedecisionlab.com/biases/primacy-effect)
91	[^12]: The Decision Lab, [Recency Effect](https://thedecisionlab.com/biases/recency-effect)
92	[^13]: Jamie Twiss, [AI Coding Degrades: Silent Failures Emerge](https://spectrum.ieee.org/ai-coding-degrades), IEEE Spectrum, January 2026
93	[^14]: OX Security, [Army of Juniors: The AI Code Security Crisis](https://www.ox.security/resource-category/whitepapers-and-reports/army-of-juniors/), October 2025
94	[^15]: Veracode, [2025 GenAI Code Security Report](https://www.veracode.com/resources/analyst-reports/2025-genai-code-security-report/), July 2025

- **Popular choice over good.** Given the choice, models default to whatever's most popular: Python over Rust, React over Svelte, the big library over the specialized one. Popularity isn't a design decision, but the model treats it like one.[^9]

In addition, Veracode's 2025 GenAI Code Security Report[^15] demonstrates that models can't simply be trained on better security principles, because security requires understanding context. Is this piece of data under system control or was it entered by an end user? Is this piece of code on an internal system or exposed to the internet?
### Your Code base
- **Blind to your domain.** The model doesn't know your business, your users, or the problem you're solving. It generates code without context for why that code needs to exist.[^10] [^7]
- **Scattered sources, incomplete picture.** Your code lives in one place, your user stories/PBIs in another, your documentation somewhere else. Even if the model has access to all of it, the connections between a specific user story and the code that implements it are hard to see. So the model never sees the full picture.[^7] [^10]
- **Context windows have a middle problem.** Even large context windows don't solve this. Models tend to lose focus on the middle, paying attention to the start and end while forgetting the parts that matter.[^10] [^7] Strangely, the model suffers from similar cognitive biases as we humans[^2], see: Primacy[^11] and Recency Effects[^12].

Some of this we try to retrofit by adding more rules or context via Claude.md or Claude/Agent skills. I.E. Explicitly telling the model about the DRY principle or giving it an outline of your project structure. However, that only goes so far. The more we stuff into the Claude.md file, the less room there is in the models context window for the code itself.

We can't wait for the labs to make this better; it will require a fundamental shift in what they focus on and how they train the models. Since that isn't happening, we need to find a way to deal with this ourselves. If someone wants to fund a better approach, I'm available. Until then, we deal with what we've got.

## What gets us out of this mess? TDD? Code Reviews?
Wow, that is a lot of issues. How do we deal with this? Contrary to a few comments, we can't code review our way out of this mess. That's putting the burden on humans to tidy up the mess that the AI created. Code reviews are so bad that they will get a blog post of their own. (See also: [The Real Cost of AI-Generated Code](/blog/the-real-cost-of-ai-generated-code-it-s-not-all-it-s-cracked-up-to-be/) and [Using GenAI to Code? Not So Fast](/blog/using-genai-to-code-not-so-fast/).) And don't get me started on the idea of LLM reviewing another LLM's output, again, that's a misunderstanding of what these tools are good for.

So what about TDD? It helps, but it's solving the wrong problem. TDD helps developers clarify *what* they're solving before *how*, by expressing understanding as small, concrete, failing tests. It's a thinking tool, not a testing tool. That makes it valuable for AI-generated code: it forces you to understand the problem before accepting the solution. But TDD operates at the code level. It can't tell you whether the feature itself is waste. I haven't seen any evidence that TDD, combined with GenAI, will reduce Technical Debt, duplication, or cognitive complexity. For a concrete example of these quality gaps in practice, see our [AI Code Generation and the Tennis Kata](/blog/ai-code-generation-and-the-tennis-kata/) experiment.

## Where Do We Go From Here?
The models won't fix themselves, and the labs aren't prioritizing what matters: well-designed architecture, maintainability, security in context, and respect for your codebase. Some of it can't be designed in the models no matter how we try.

The Shift Left movement has always had the right idea: Continuous Discovery, Lean Startup Experiments, Lean UX, and real BDD (i.e., collaboration on examples). The job is to build great products, not blindly shovel more defect-laden code into production. When teams [automate away collaboration in favour of speed](/blog/gen-ai-and-the-feature-factory-automating-away-collaboration/), these quality problems compound.

When it comes to the code itself, give the models smaller, more focused tasks. Start with a small set of acceptance criteria for a single feature and work from there.

Instead of trying to do a better job of building quality into code faster. Why don't we work on making sure we know what the right product is first? What are you doing to survive this mess? I genuinely want to know.

In our [Certified ScrumMaster workshops](/courses/certified-scrummaster-csm-training/), we practice building teams that focus on collaboration and quality over raw output.

## LLM Usage Note
Parallel.AI for research, NotebookLLM to ground-check claims against source material, and Gemini via Obsidian Copilot for writing critique. Claude Code helps turn the markdown text into mdx file for a blog post.

[^1]: CodeRabbit, [State of the AI vs. Human Code Generation Report](https://www.coderabbit.ai/whitepapers/state-of-AI-vs-human-code-generation-report)
[^2]: Adam Tauman Kalai, Ofir Nachum, Santosh S. Vempala, and Edwin Zhang, [Why Language Models Hallucinate](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2509.04664.pdf)
[^3]: Robin Gröpler et al., [The Future of Generative AI in Software Engineering: A Vision from Industry and Academia in the European GENIUS Project](https://arxiv.org/html/2511.01348v2)
[^4]: Kaushik Bar, [AI for Code Synthesis: Can LLMs Generate Secure Code?](https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=5157837)
[^5]: Shuai Wang, Liang Ding, Li Shen, Yong Luo, Bo Du, and Dacheng Tao, [OOP: Object-Oriented Programming Evaluation Benchmark for Large Language Models](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2401.06628.pdf)
[^6]: Mootez Saad, José Antonio Hernández López, Boqi Chen, Neil Ernst, Dániel Varró, and Tushar Sharma, [SENAI: Towards Software Engineering Native Generative Artificial Intelligence](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2503.15282.pdf)
[^7]: Jiessie Tie, Bingsheng Yao, Tianshi Li, Syed Ishtiaque Ahmed, Dakuo Wang, and Shurui Zhou, [LLMs are Imperfect, Then What? An Empirical Study on LLM Failures in Software Engineering](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2411.09916.pdf)
[^8]: Manish Bhatt, Sahana Chennabasappa, Cyrus Nikolaidis et al., [Purple Llama CyberSecEval: A Secure Coding Benchmark for Language Models](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2312.04724.pdf)
[^9]: Lukas Twist, Jie M. Zhang, Mark Harman, Don Syme, Joost Noppen, Helen Yannakoudakis, and Detlef Nauck, [A Study of LLMs' Preferences for Libraries and Programming Languages](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2503.17181.pdf)
[^10]: Cuiyun Gao, Xing Hu, Shan Gao, Xin Xia, and Zhi Jin, [The Current Challenges of Software Engineering in the Era of Large Language Models](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2412.14554.pdf)
[^11]: The Decision Lab, [Primacy Effect](https://thedecisionlab.com/biases/primacy-effect)
[^12]: The Decision Lab, [Recency Effect](https://thedecisionlab.com/biases/recency-effect)
[^13]: Jamie Twiss, [AI Coding Degrades: Silent Failures Emerge](https://spectrum.ieee.org/ai-coding-degrades), IEEE Spectrum, January 2026
[^14]: OX Security, [Army of Juniors: The AI Code Security Crisis](https://www.ox.security/resource-category/whitepapers-and-reports/army-of-juniors/), October 2025
[^15]: Veracode, [2025 GenAI Code Security Report](https://www.veracode.com/resources/analyst-reports/2025-genai-code-security-report/), July 2025

1	---
2	title: "The Sprint Backlog: A Truly Complete Guide with Examples"
3	date: "2023-11-08"
4	lastUpdated: '2025-05-01'
5	categories:
6	  - "scrum-events-and-artifacts"
7	coverImage: "@/content/blog/the-humble-sprint-backlog/images/2017CSM-Sample-Scrum-Task-Board-v2-895x1024.jpg"
8	excerpt: 'Good Scrum teams know that they own the Sprint Backlog. Great teams experiment.'
9	---
10	
11	import Figure from '@/components/global/figure.astro';
12	import CSMSampleScrumTaskBoardV2895x1024 from '@/content/blog/the-humble-sprint-backlog/images/2017CSM-Sample-Scrum-Task-Board-v2-895x1024.jpg';
13	import CSMSampleScrumTaskBoard3 from '@/content/blog/the-humble-sprint-backlog/images/2019CSM-Sample-Scrum-Task-Board_3.jpg';
14	import ASameerBendre2300x225 from '@/content/blog/the-humble-sprint-backlog/images/ASameerBendre-2-300x225.jpg';
15	import DavidKoontzPainFreeDentalMarketing300x225 from '@/content/blog/the-humble-sprint-backlog/images/DavidKoontz-PainFreeDental-Marketing-300x225.jpg';
16	import SameerBendre1300x225 from '@/content/blog/the-humble-sprint-backlog/images/SameerBendre-1-300x225.jpg';
17	
18	
19	We might not be able to make Sprint Backlogs exciting, but we can make them more effective. Let's look at what a Sprint Backlog is, what purpose it serves, and how to create, manage, and improve it.
20	
21	## What is a Sprint Backlog?
22	
23	A Sprint Backlog is a list of Product Backlog Items (PBIs) that the Developers think they can complete during the Sprint, along with the work needed, described in small enough chunks (e.g. User Stories) that progress can be tracked throughout the Sprint. These items are selected from the Product Backlog by the Scrum Team during Sprint Planning.
24	
25	The Sprint Backlog is essential because it is the Team's clear plan for how to achieve the Sprint Goal that they committed to for the Sprint. The team's work is visible and updated on a daily basis to encourage transparency and collaboration within the team itself. By having a clear plan for the Sprint, it allows the team to focus and bring the highest value work to completion.
26	
27	## Who creates the Sprint Backlog?
28	
29	The Scrum Team is responsible for creating the Sprint Backlog. Sadly, many Scrum Teams simply use whatever their online Scrum tool feeds them for their Sprint Backlog. This harms the Team's capacity for engagement because it reinforces the sense that Scrum is _happening to them_, not something that _they choose_.
30	
31	Since the Sprint Backlog is solely for the use of the Scrum Team to organize their own work during a Sprint, they are the only ones who create, change, and manage it — not a tool, and not an outsider.
32	
33	### When is the Sprint Backlog created?
34	
35	The Sprint Backlog is created in the Sprint Planning session at the beginning of each Sprint. Prior to the start of the Sprint the Product Owner has prioritized the items and discussed them with the team (this is called Product Backlog Refinement). By doing it before Sprint Planning, the whole team better understand what they're committing to. This collaborative effort ensures shared understanding and ownership of the Sprint Backlog. During the Sprint, the Sprint Backlog is updated by the Scrum Team when something changes, a task or Product backlog Item (PBI) is completed, or a new item is started.
36	
37	## How does a Sprint Backlog work?
38	
39	After the Scrum Team creates the Sprint Backlog, the Developers (Scrum's poor way of saying all the people who do work) break down the Product Backlog Items (PBI) into smaller size and estimating the work needed, the team works through the Sprint Backlog with each individual team member selecting PBIs to work on. This promotes autonomy and allows Developers to work on things they feel most comfortable with or have the necessary expertise in. As a PBI is completed, the Scrum Team updates the Sprint Backlog to reflect that. There is no required work order for items. Since the Scrum Team is truly self-organizing, they could work on the Sprint Backlog in whatever order they see fit, but effective teams usually work from highest to lowest priority.
40	
41	### How should the Sprint Backlog be managed?
42	
43	Since we look at the Sprint Backlog during Daily Scrum, most Scrum teams update it there. The frequent visibility and review are intended to improve transparency and collaboration among team members. No one is assigned work in Scrum, instead, team members have the freedom to choose what they want to work on themselves, so any team member may update a Sprint Backlog item. They might mark it as done, or as needing feedback from the Product Owner, etc. If a particular item in the Sprint Backlog is confusing:
44	
45	1. it should not be brought into the Sprint and, instead, turned into a conversation at the next refinement session, or
46	2. it can be turned into a Spike – a timeboxed investigative effort to better understand the problem, or
47	3. t can be committed pending further clarification right after Sprint Planning. (This is a common practice and is almost always a bad idea. Options 1 and 2 are better choices).
48	
49	A Sprint is dynamic and evolves so the Sprint Backlog changes as the Sprint moves along. The Sprint plan that helped you start the Sprint often doesn't last the whole Sprint. Did the team realize that a User Story (aka PBI) won't be completed this Sprint? Remove it and tell the Product Owner. Hit by a product support defect mid-Sprint? Add the emergency fix to the Sprint Backlog, or put an existing item on hold and swarm the defect. (_Hint: if this is a frequent problem, we've covered reducing the Production Support burden in this [Scrum By Example entry](/blog/scrum-production-support/)_).
50	
51	#### Fixed Scope or Variable Scope?
52	
53	People get themselves tied up in endless knots on this subject – are the contents of the Sprint fixed (i.e. Fixed Scope) or can they change (Variable Scope)? These notes won't settle all debates, but they should help reduce them.
54	
55	- [Sprint Goal](/blog/sprint-goals-provide-purpose/) – This shouldn't change during the Sprint.
56	- Product Items committed to the Sprint – If the Sprint isn't going well, the team might drop an item. On rare occasions when something important is discovered by the PO, the Scrum Team might accept a new PBI mid-Sprint. _My normal recommendation is that they remove a larger existing item to accommodate the new item. I would expect the Team to discuss in their subsequent retrospective what happened and how to ensure that it doesn't happen again._
57	- Task Items – Any amount of change is fine here since tasks aren't officially part of Scrum and the task list can change on a daily basis.
58	
59	If change is made to the work in Sprint, it needs to come through the shared agreement and collaborative understanding of the team, not as something imposed from the outside.
60	
61	## What are the characteristics of a Sprint Backlog?
62	
63	The _Scrum Guide_ doesn't provide any guidance on the structure or format of a Sprint Backlog: "The Sprint Backlog is a plan by and for the Developers. It is a highly visible, real-time picture of the work that the Developers plan to accomplish during the Sprint in order to achieve the Sprint Goal."[^1]
64	
65	**Since Teams are unique, there is no single correct practice that they all should follow when creating a Sprint Backlog.** Teams choose and experiment with whatever helps them most to stay focused and self-organize, creating the Sprint Backlog with whatever methods work best for them, such as index cards, whiteboards, or, yes, even electronic tool.
66	
67	The Sprint Backlog is created by the Team, for the Team, so there are no set-in-stone rules. If your Team wants it to include a XKCD comic, go for it. That said, there are some things that people have found to be effective, so they're worthwhile considering.
68	
69	### Swim Lanes and Columns
70	
71	To keep the board organized visually, Teams use horizontal swim lanes and vertical columns to create a rough grid. At the front of a swim lane is their Product Backlog Item (e.g. User Story or task). Then there is a series of columns moving left to right (instinctive to how we read English text), indicating progress of that Backlog Item through the Sprint.
72	
73	When teams transition from traditional project management methods, they might be tempted to use the Sprint Backlog to recreate familiar phases such as Analysis, Design, Development, and Test. Teams do this, but it misses the collaborative nature of Scrum and introduces unnecessary handoffs between team members.
74	
75	#### **Example Sprint Backlog 1:**
76	
77	<Figure
78	  src={CSMSampleScrumTaskBoardV2895x1024}
79	  alt="Illustration of a sprint backlog board, with various placeholder columns and sticky notes"
80	  caption="Illustration of a sprint backlog board, with various placeholder columns and sticky notes"
81	/>
82	
83	To someone new to the Agile world the picture above may look a bit alien. Let's break it down further and make sense of it.
84	
85	### Does a Sprint Backlog have tasks – yes or no?
86	
87	Tasks are not a required element of the Sprint Backlog. If tasks are included, it's recommended that they're decomposed into parts small enough to be completed in a day or less, so that Team members can share tangible progress on a daily basis. If the PBIs are already very small – perhaps completed by two people in a couple of days – then breaking them down further into tasks is probably not productive.
88	
89	### "Finished" or "Complete" vs "Story Accepted"
90	
91	If a Team does put tasks on the Sprint Backlog, they might find it helpful to create a boundary between tasks that the Team members themselves declare finished, and the User Story/PBI being accepted by the Product Owner.
92	
93	### Work in Progress
94	
95	Many Teams benefit by stealing a page from the Kanban playbook and limiting Work in Progress, then including that in their Sprint Backlog structure. To sense whether they're on track to meet the Sprint Goal, they simply look at the number of completed PBIs. If by the third or fourth day of a ten-day Sprint there isn't at least one item finished, then it's unlikely that the Team will get everything completed by Sprint end. By the sixth or seventh day, we would expect a Team to have at least half the items complete.[^3]
96	
97	Teams that limit Work in Progress to only two or three Product Backlog Items at one time, tend to:
98	
99	- collaborate more. They often discover practices like Behaviour Driven Development (or BDD) and Pair Programming. In the long run, these teams improve their throughput.
100	- cross-skill faster, since the bottlenecks become self-evident.
101	- eventually eliminate the problem of having unfinished work at the end of Sprint. If you limit WIP and you're only a few days away from the end of the Sprint, then the team could swarm the remaining work one chunk at a time, making it likely that there will be no unfinished work at the end of Sprint.
102	
103	So, used well, a Sprint Backlog combined with the Kanban WIP limit can solve challenges that many teams face.
104	
105	### Bringing Retrospective into the Sprint Backlog
106	
107	The example Team has also put a swim lane at the top for their actions or improvements that they committed to in the [Sprint Retrospective](/guide-to-effective-agile-retrospectives/). It's at the top of the picture to act as a visual reminder that continually improving their process and Team is important. It's recommended that the Developers include at least one action item from their previous Sprint's Retrospective.
108	
109	### Adding the Sprint Goal
110	
111	Finally, the Team in our above example has placed their Sprint Goal atop the Sprint Backlog as a visual reminder that it is the overarching goal of the Sprint, rather than just finishing individual tasks.
112	
113	These additions encourage the Team to focus on more than just delivering a collection of User Stories. Instead, they're achieving the Sprint Goal while making improvements that, in the mid-term, help increase their work quality and effectiveness.
114	
115	This next Team has a slightly different view of the world, so it's appropriate that their Sprint Backlog looks different as well.
116	
117	<Figure
118	  src={CSMSampleScrumTaskBoard3}
119	  alt="illustration of an example sprint backlog, with different lanes for different aspects of work"
120	  caption="illustration of an example sprint backlog, with different lanes for different aspects of work"
121	/>
122	
123	
124	The Team above has a product live in the field. They have added a swim lane to visualize Production Support work as a separate activity in their Sprint Backlog.
125	
126	#### Real Life Examples of a Sprint Backlog
127	
128	The above two examples are obviously graphics created to illustrate common Sprint Backlog structure. Here are some photos of actual Sprint Backlogs, and you can click on the smaller photos to open full-size images.
129	
130	<Figure
131	  src={ASameerBendre2300x225}
132	  alt="Photo of a whiteboard with a sprint backlog on it, featuring multiple lanes"
133	  caption="Photo of a whiteboard with a sprint backlog on it, featuring multiple lanes"
134	/>
135	] Image courtesy of Sameer Bendre.
136	
137	**Sprint Backlog Example 3:** This Team has Expedite Lanes at the top, and column headings include "Challenge", "Analysis and Planning" and "Unit Test".
138	
139	<Figure
140	  src={DavidKoontzPainFreeDentalMarketing300x225}
141	  alt="Photo of a Sprint Backlog board, with a unique Calls column"
142	  caption="Photo of a Sprint Backlog board, with a unique Calls column"
143	/>
144	Image courtesy of [David Koontz](https://t.co/TsWPt6402B?amp=1).
145	
146	<Figure
147	  src={SameerBendre1300x225}
148	  alt="Photo of a sprint backlog on a white board, with team-unique columns"
149	  caption="Photo of a sprint backlog on a white board, with team-unique columns"
150	/>
151	 Image courtesy of Sameer Bendre.
152	
153	**Sprint Backlog Example 5:** This Team has chosen columns for "WIP" (Work in Progress), "Ready for CR" and "In CR", "Validate in Prod", and "Closed in TFS".
154	
155	_Some of these examples might have contents that make no sense to you, or your environment, and that's okay. They don't have to, because a Sprint Backlog has to only make sense for the Team that created it._
156	
157	### More Ideas for Your Sprint Backlog
158	
159	Here are other things you might try for the structure and contents of your Sprint Backlog, based on what some Scrum Teams have found effective for them. Remember, your mileage may vary, so experiment and make it your own.
160	
161	- Put **tick marks** on a card for every day it has been worked on and a 'B' for everyday it was blocked/stuck. _This helps the team by providing information on how long individual work items took to complete, or how long they got delayed. Most teams discover that work items often spend longer waiting for something (approvals,  another team, etc …) than they do getting worked on._
162	- Create a separate column for items that are **Stuck/Waiting For/Blocked** and make a note of the why. _A separate "Waiting For" column visualizes the blockages in the system. Visualization makes them easier to measure, and attracts greater attention to resolve them sooner. After all, our teams don't want to measure blockages, rather we want blocked items unblocked as soon as possible._
163	- Track **Interruptions** (e.g. management requests), requests for help from another Team... basically, track anything that causes the Team to lose focus on the Sprint Goal. _These are usually tracked in their own lane. By tracking them, it highlights opportunities to work to reduce them._
164	- Create an **Impediments** area to track open and resolved impediments. _This helps the team see where their problems are. During the retrospective, these impediments can make fodder for good discussion._
165	- Have a visual reminder of the **Definition of Done** on the boundary between Finished (for a task) and Accepted (for a User Story). _This helps the team by making them think about the meaning of Done and therefore what level of quality is expected._
166	- Some teams that use **Tasks** find it useful to create task items that correspond to the Definition of Done. Other teams find that keeping the Definition visible at all times is a sufficient reminder.
167	- **Hidden or Ghost work**[^2] – Sometimes we discover that team members are working on things outside of the Sprint Backlog. On discovery in Daily Scrum (or any other time), make it visible. Many teams use the interruptions lane above, since this work from outside the Sprint Backlog is an interruption.
168	- Include a **Calendar** to note vacations, birthdays, special events, etc – anything that might affect the time available for work, as well as morale. _Being reminded of our peers' schedules and lives makes them more relatable. On a simple practical level, seeing a teammate's upcoming vacation plans reminds us to address questions before they disappear, minimizing the number of items that get blocked by their absence._
169	- Consider noting any other **events** that affect the Team during the Sprint, _e.g. an all hands meeting, other meetings,[^4]  server outage, Zoom or MS Teams outage._
170	- Track **mood, energy, etc** using something as a simple as a spreadsheet view with people's names in rows, calendar/weekdays across the top. _On a daily basis, they mark happiness, satisfaction, engagement or some other simple measure, which will help document whether the Team's energy or focus was negatively impacted.[^5]_
171	
172	All of the information that the Team tracks via the Sprint Backlog becomes data that should be brought into the Sprint Retrospective.
173	
174	When your Sprint Backlog is designed and prepopulated by an outsider (or an electronic tool), it's unlikely to contain any of these improvements that can help make the Backlog – and what it tells you – more effective and informative. But at the end of the day, if a tool helps the team improve collaboration and focus, then it is useful.
175	
176	(Note, if having to maintain a tool for the Sprint Backlog slows down the Team, that is an impediment and it's up to the ScrumMaster to help find a better solution.)
177	
178	## Sprint Backlog: End of Sprint
179	
180	The Sprint Backlog is reviewed during Sprint Review at the end of the Sprint. The Sprint Backlog is finished and completed work is deployed. The Sprint Backlog cards can now be disposed. (One team I worked with archived them in a shoebox and put a rubber band around each Sprint's worth. Honestly, I don't think anyone ever looked at them again.)
181	
182	What happens to incomplete work in a Sprint Backlog? It is returned to the Product Backlog wherever the Product Owner deems it belongs. In the next Sprint Planning session, a new Sprint Backlog is created.
183	
184	## Sprint Backlog Anti-Patterns
185	
186	(aka Avoid Doing These)
187	
188	#### Pre-assignment
189	
190	When the Sprint Backlog is created during Sprint Planning, some teams decide who will work on which PBI or task. When it's kept to only one item, this isn't bad, however when all items are pre-assigned to team members, we have just planned for the first bottleneck.
191	
192	#### One Person Doing Many Things
193	
194	This happens when Team Members are signed up for one than one task or PBI at the same time. We can't multitask like we think we can because our brains just haven't evolved to do this. The more we multitask, the less we get done overall. So when Team Members sign up for more than one task at a time, they're promising to get less done. _Exception: if a team member has one item stuck in Blocked (or Waiting for), they might start work on another. If it happens again, the team should look into why one person's work is so frequently blocked. Alternative: when a team member has a item blocked, they might pair with another team member to help that person through the item._
195	
196	#### Reporting
197	
198	The Sprint Backlog loses its value if used for external purposes like reporting, or for [micro-management](/blog/scrum-anti-patterns-micromanagement/). When leadership uses it to look over the shoulders of the people doing the work — even if it's not to direct the Development Team's actions — it often leads to overloading the Sprint Backlog with details that undermine and eliminate transparency. The Sprint Backlog is used only by the Scrum team, and is not intended to be viewed by anyone else.
199	
200	#### Multiple Sprints
201	
202	Since Scrum is about adapting to the evolving work, it is pointless to plan which items will go into the Sprint Backlog beyond the current Sprint, so we shouldn't try to create Sprint Backlogs in advance. _I think this happens because some of the popular electronic tools make it possible and people assume, based on the tool, that this is a good practice._ Planning future Sprints before they happen reduces flexibility and increases workload for all involved. For a related rant on why adopting the tool doesn't make an organization Agile, see [JIRA is Not Agile](/blog/jira-is-not-agile/).
203	
204	#### Phases
205	
206	When people come from a traditional world into Scrum, some try to use the Sprint Backlog as a tool to recreate the phases they're used to. For example, they create columns in their Sprint Backlog for Analysis; Design; Development; Test. _While strictly speaking legal, they're recreating the boundaries between traditional roles, making collaboration less likely and ensuring handoffs between team members. As mentioned in the Limiting WIP segment, effective Teams work collaboratively through the Sprint to get a PBI to complete before moving onto the next. These phases tend to lead to another Scrum sin – Staggered Sprints._
207	
208	## Forecasting with the Sprint Backlog
209	
210	The Sprint Backlog is also the Developers' forecasting tool. Each day during [Daily Scrum](/blog/modern-guide-to-daily-scrum-meeting/), they replan their work and update the Sprint Backlog , using it to help them assess whether they're on track to meet their Sprint Goal. If they realize that their Sprint Goal is in jeopardy, they work with the Product Owner on replanning.
211	
212	In the past, Teams used to use a [Sprint Burndown Chart](/blog/scrummaster-tales-the-trouble-with-sprint-burndowns/) that tracked task hours remaining to be done. Now, most of us would suggest that the focus on Tasks, versus focusing on User Stories/PBIs, is anti-pattern so we don't recommend Sprint Burndowns.
213	
214	## Sprint Backlog vs Kanban Wall vs Product Backlog
215	
216	While the Sprint Backlog is the Team's plan for the Sprint, the Product Backlog is the Teams queue of work. So the funny thing is that the Sprint Backlog and Product Backlog have easily confused names, but vastly different meanings. In my [workshops](/choose-the-right-scrum-training-for-your-needs/), whenever an attendee answers a question with, "Backlog", my instant response is, "Which one?"
217	
218	A Sprint Backlog is far more like the (better-named) Kanban board. A Kanban board is a visual control system from the world of Kanban. It combines the Product Backlog with the Sprint Backlog.
