---
title: "The Sprint Backlog: A Truly Complete Guide with Examples"
date: "2023-11-08"
lastUpdated: '2025-05-01'
categories:
  - "scrum-events-and-artifacts"
coverImage: "@/content/blog/the-humble-sprint-backlog/images/2017CSM-Sample-Scrum-Task-Board-v2-895x1024.jpg"
excerpt: 'Good Scrum teams know that they own the Sprint Backlog. Great teams experiment.'
---

import Figure from '@/components/global/figure.astro';
import CSMSampleScrumTaskBoardV2895x1024 from '@/content/blog/the-humble-sprint-backlog/images/2017CSM-Sample-Scrum-Task-Board-v2-895x1024.jpg';
import CSMSampleScrumTaskBoard3 from '@/content/blog/the-humble-sprint-backlog/images/2019CSM-Sample-Scrum-Task-Board_3.jpg';
import ASameerBendre2300x225 from '@/content/blog/the-humble-sprint-backlog/images/ASameerBendre-2-300x225.jpg';
import DavidKoontzPainFreeDentalMarketing300x225 from '@/content/blog/the-humble-sprint-backlog/images/DavidKoontz-PainFreeDental-Marketing-300x225.jpg';
import SameerBendre1300x225 from '@/content/blog/the-humble-sprint-backlog/images/SameerBendre-1-300x225.jpg';


We might not be able to make Sprint Backlogs exciting, but we can make them more effective. Let's look at what a Sprint Backlog is, what purpose it serves, and how to create, manage, and improve it.

## What is a Sprint Backlog?

A Sprint Backlog is a list of Product Backlog Items (PBIs) that the Developers think they can complete during the Sprint, along with the work needed, described in small enough chunks (e.g. User Stories) that progress can be tracked throughout the Sprint. These items are selected from the Product Backlog by the Scrum Team during Sprint Planning.

The Sprint Backlog is essential because it is the Team's clear plan for how to achieve the Sprint Goal that they committed to for the Sprint. The team's work is visible and updated on a daily basis to encourage transparency and collaboration within the team itself. By having a clear plan for the Sprint, it allows the team to focus and bring the highest value work to completion.

## Who creates the Sprint Backlog?

The Scrum Team is responsible for creating the Sprint Backlog. Sadly, many Scrum Teams simply use whatever their online Scrum tool feeds them for their Sprint Backlog. This harms the Team's capacity for engagement because it reinforces the sense that Scrum is _happening to them_, not something that _they choose_.

Since the Sprint Backlog is solely for the use of the Scrum Team to organize their own work during a Sprint, they are the only ones who create, change, and manage it — not a tool, and not an outsider.

### When is the Sprint Backlog created?

The Sprint Backlog is created in the Sprint Planning session at the beginning of each Sprint. Prior to the start of the Sprint the Product Owner has prioritized the items and discussed them with the team (this is called Product Backlog Refinement). By doing it before Sprint Planning, the whole team better understand what they're committing to. This collaborative effort ensures shared understanding and ownership of the Sprint Backlog. During the Sprint, the Sprint Backlog is updated by the Scrum Team when something changes, a task or Product backlog Item (PBI) is completed, or a new item is started.

## How does a Sprint Backlog work?

After the Scrum Team creates the Sprint Backlog, the Developers (Scrum's poor way of saying all the people who do work) break down the Product Backlog Items (PBI) into smaller size and estimating the work needed, the team works through the Sprint Backlog with each individual team member selecting PBIs to work on. This promotes autonomy and allows Developers to work on things they feel most comfortable with or have the necessary expertise in. As a PBI is completed, the Scrum Team updates the Sprint Backlog to reflect that. There is no required work order for items. Since the Scrum Team is truly self-organizing, they could work on the Sprint Backlog in whatever order they see fit, but effective teams usually work from highest to lowest priority.

### How should the Sprint Backlog be managed?

Since we look at the Sprint Backlog during Daily Scrum, most Scrum teams update it there. The frequent visibility and review are intended to improve transparency and collaboration among team members. No one is assigned work in Scrum, instead, team members have the freedom to choose what they want to work on themselves, so any team member may update a Sprint Backlog item. They might mark it as done, or as needing feedback from the Product Owner, etc. If a particular item in the Sprint Backlog is confusing:

1. it should not be brought into the Sprint and, instead, turned into a conversation at the next refinement session, or
2. it can be turned into a Spike – a timeboxed investigative effort to better understand the problem, or
3. t can be committed pending further clarification right after Sprint Planning. (This is a common practice and is almost always a bad idea. Options 1 and 2 are better choices).

A Sprint is dynamic and evolves so the Sprint Backlog changes as the Sprint moves along. The Sprint plan that helped you start the Sprint often doesn't last the whole Sprint. Did the team realize that a User Story (aka PBI) won't be completed this Sprint? Remove it and tell the Product Owner. Hit by a product support defect mid-Sprint? Add the emergency fix to the Sprint Backlog, or put an existing item on hold and swarm the defect. (_Hint: if this is a frequent problem, we've covered reducing the Production Support burden in this [Scrum By Example entry](/blog/scrum-production-support/)_).

#### Fixed Scope or Variable Scope?

People get themselves tied up in endless knots on this subject – are the contents of the Sprint fixed (i.e. Fixed Scope) or can they change (Variable Scope)? These notes won't settle all debates, but they should help reduce them.

- [Sprint Goal](/blog/sprint-goals-provide-purpose/) – This shouldn't change during the Sprint.
- Product Items committed to the Sprint – If the Sprint isn't going well, the team might drop an item. On rare occasions when something important is discovered by the PO, the Scrum Team might accept a new PBI mid-Sprint. _My normal recommendation is that they remove a larger existing item to accommodate the new item. I would expect the Team to discuss in their subsequent retrospective what happened and how to ensure that it doesn't happen again._
- Task Items – Any amount of change is fine here since tasks aren't officially part of Scrum and the task list can change on a daily basis.

If change is made to the work in Sprint, it needs to come through the shared agreement and collaborative understanding of the team, not as something imposed from the outside.

## What are the characteristics of a Sprint Backlog?

The _Scrum Guide_ doesn't provide any guidance on the structure or format of a Sprint Backlog: "The Sprint Backlog is a plan by and for the Developers. It is a highly visible, real-time picture of the work that the Developers plan to accomplish during the Sprint in order to achieve the Sprint Goal."[^1]

**Since Teams are unique, there is no single correct practice that they all should follow when creating a Sprint Backlog.** Teams choose and experiment with whatever helps them most to stay focused and self-organize, creating the Sprint Backlog with whatever methods work best for them, such as index cards, whiteboards, or, yes, even electronic tool.

The Sprint Backlog is created by the Team, for the Team, so there are no set-in-stone rules. If your Team wants it to include a XKCD comic, go for it. That said, there are some things that people have found to be effective, so they're worthwhile considering.

### Swim Lanes and Columns

To keep the board organized visually, Teams use horizontal swim lanes and vertical columns to create a rough grid. At the front of a swim lane is their Product Backlog Item (e.g. User Story or task). Then there is a series of columns moving left to right (instinctive to how we read English text), indicating progress of that Backlog Item through the Sprint.

When teams transition from traditional project management methods, they might be tempted to use the Sprint Backlog to recreate familiar phases such as Analysis, Design, Development, and Test. Teams do this, but it misses the collaborative nature of Scrum and introduces unnecessary handoffs between team members.

#### **Example Sprint Backlog 1:**

<Figure
  src={CSMSampleScrumTaskBoardV2895x1024}
  alt="Illustration of a sprint backlog board, with various placeholder columns and sticky notes"
  caption="Illustration of a sprint backlog board, with various placeholder columns and sticky notes"
/>

To someone new to the Agile world the picture above may look a bit alien. Let's break it down further and make sense of it.

### Does a Sprint Backlog have tasks – yes or no?

Tasks are not a required element of the Sprint Backlog. If tasks are included, it's recommended that they're decomposed into parts small enough to be completed in a day or less, so that Team members can share tangible progress on a daily basis. If the PBIs are already very small – perhaps completed by two people in a couple of days – then breaking them down further into tasks is probably not productive.

### "Finished" or "Complete" vs "Story Accepted"

If a Team does put tasks on the Sprint Backlog, they might find it helpful to create a boundary between tasks that the Team members themselves declare finished, and the User Story/PBI being accepted by the Product Owner.

### Work in Progress

Many Teams benefit by stealing a page from the Kanban playbook and limiting Work in Progress, then including that in their Sprint Backlog structure. To sense whether they're on track to meet the Sprint Goal, they simply look at the number of completed PBIs. If by the third or fourth day of a ten-day Sprint there isn't at least one item finished, then it's unlikely that the Team will get everything completed by Sprint end. By the sixth or seventh day, we would expect a Team to have at least half the items complete.[^3]

Teams that limit Work in Progress to only two or three Product Backlog Items at one time, tend to:

- collaborate more. They often discover practices like Behaviour Driven Development (or BDD) and Pair Programming. In the long run, these teams improve their throughput.
- cross-skill faster, since the bottlenecks become self-evident.
- eventually eliminate the problem of having unfinished work at the end of Sprint. If you limit WIP and you're only a few days away from the end of the Sprint, then the team could swarm the remaining work one chunk at a time, making it likely that there will be no unfinished work at the end of Sprint.

So, used well, a Sprint Backlog combined with the Kanban WIP limit can solve challenges that many teams face.

### Bringing Retrospective into the Sprint Backlog

The example Team has also put a swim lane at the top for their actions or improvements that they committed to in the [Sprint Retrospective](/guide-to-effective-agile-retrospectives/). It's at the top of the picture to act as a visual reminder that continually improving their process and Team is important. It's recommended that the Developers include at least one action item from their previous Sprint's Retrospective.

### Adding the Sprint Goal

Finally, the Team in our above example has placed their Sprint Goal atop the Sprint Backlog as a visual reminder that it is the overarching goal of the Sprint, rather than just finishing individual tasks.

These additions encourage the Team to focus on more than just delivering a collection of User Stories. Instead, they're achieving the Sprint Goal while making improvements that, in the mid-term, help increase their work quality and effectiveness.

This next Team has a slightly different view of the world, so it's appropriate that their Sprint Backlog looks different as well.

<Figure
  src={CSMSampleScrumTaskBoard3}
  alt="illustration of an example sprint backlog, with different lanes for different aspects of work"
  caption="illustration of an example sprint backlog, with different lanes for different aspects of work"
/>


The Team above has a product live in the field. They have added a swim lane to visualize Production Support work as a separate activity in their Sprint Backlog.

#### Real Life Examples of a Sprint Backlog

The above two examples are obviously graphics created to illustrate common Sprint Backlog structure. Here are some photos of actual Sprint Backlogs, and you can click on the smaller photos to open full-size images.

<Figure
  src={ASameerBendre2300x225}
  alt="Photo of a whiteboard with a sprint backlog on it, featuring multiple lanes"
  caption="Photo of a whiteboard with a sprint backlog on it, featuring multiple lanes"
/>
] Image courtesy of Sameer Bendre.

**Sprint Backlog Example 3:** This Team has Expedite Lanes at the top, and column headings include "Challenge", "Analysis and Planning" and "Unit Test".

<Figure
  src={DavidKoontzPainFreeDentalMarketing300x225}
  alt="Photo of a Sprint Backlog board, with a unique Calls column"
  caption="Photo of a Sprint Backlog board, with a unique Calls column"
/>
Image courtesy of [David Koontz](https://t.co/TsWPt6402B?amp=1).

<Figure
  src={SameerBendre1300x225}
  alt="Photo of a sprint backlog on a white board, with team-unique columns"
  caption="Photo of a sprint backlog on a white board, with team-unique columns"
/>
 Image courtesy of Sameer Bendre.

**Sprint Backlog Example 5:** This Team has chosen columns for "WIP" (Work in Progress), "Ready for CR" and "In CR", "Validate in Prod", and "Closed in TFS".

_Some of these examples might have contents that make no sense to you, or your environment, and that's okay. They don't have to, because a Sprint Backlog has to only make sense for the Team that created it._

### More Ideas for Your Sprint Backlog

Here are other things you might try for the structure and contents of your Sprint Backlog, based on what some Scrum Teams have found effective for them. Remember, your mileage may vary, so experiment and make it your own.

- Put **tick marks** on a card for every day it has been worked on and a 'B' for everyday it was blocked/stuck. _This helps the team by providing information on how long individual work items took to complete, or how long they got delayed. Most teams discover that work items often spend longer waiting for something (approvals,  another team, etc …) than they do getting worked on._
- Create a separate column for items that are **Stuck/Waiting For/Blocked** and make a note of the why. _A separate "Waiting For" column visualizes the blockages in the system. Visualization makes them easier to measure, and attracts greater attention to resolve them sooner. After all, our teams don't want to measure blockages, rather we want blocked items unblocked as soon as possible._
- Track **Interruptions** (e.g. management requests), requests for help from another Team... basically, track anything that causes the Team to lose focus on the Sprint Goal. _These are usually tracked in their own lane. By tracking them, it highlights opportunities to work to reduce them._
- Create an **Impediments** area to track open and resolved impediments. _This helps the team see where their problems are. During the retrospective, these impediments can make fodder for good discussion._
- Have a visual reminder of the **Definition of Done** on the boundary between Finished (for a task) and Accepted (for a User Story). _This helps the team by making them think about the meaning of Done and therefore what level of quality is expected._
- Some teams that use **Tasks** find it useful to create task items that correspond to the Definition of Done. Other teams find that keeping the Definition visible at all times is a sufficient reminder.
- **Hidden or Ghost work**[^2] – Sometimes we discover that team members are working on things outside of the Sprint Backlog. On discovery in Daily Scrum (or any other time), make it visible. Many teams use the interruptions lane above, since this work from outside the Sprint Backlog is an interruption.
- Include a **Calendar** to note vacations, birthdays, special events, etc – anything that might affect the time available for work, as well as morale. _Being reminded of our peers' schedules and lives makes them more relatable. On a simple practical level, seeing a teammate's upcoming vacation plans reminds us to address questions before they disappear, minimizing the number of items that get blocked by their absence._
- Consider noting any other **events** that affect the Team during the Sprint, _e.g. an all hands meeting, other meetings,[^4]  server outage, Zoom or MS Teams outage._
- Track **mood, energy, etc** using something as a simple as a spreadsheet view with people's names in rows, calendar/weekdays across the top. _On a daily basis, they mark happiness, satisfaction, engagement or some other simple measure, which will help document whether the Team's energy or focus was negatively impacted.[^5]_

All of the information that the Team tracks via the Sprint Backlog becomes data that should be brought into the Sprint Retrospective.

When your Sprint Backlog is designed and prepopulated by an outsider (or an electronic tool), it's unlikely to contain any of these improvements that can help make the Backlog – and what it tells you – more effective and informative. But at the end of the day, if a tool helps the team improve collaboration and focus, then it is useful.

(Note, if having to maintain a tool for the Sprint Backlog slows down the Team, that is an impediment and it's up to the ScrumMaster to help find a better solution.)

## Sprint Backlog: End of Sprint

The Sprint Backlog is reviewed during Sprint Review at the end of the Sprint. The Sprint Backlog is finished and completed work is deployed. The Sprint Backlog cards can now be disposed. (One team I worked with archived them in a shoebox and put a rubber band around each Sprint's worth. Honestly, I don't think anyone ever looked at them again.)

What happens to incomplete work in a Sprint Backlog? It is returned to the Product Backlog wherever the Product Owner deems it belongs. In the next Sprint Planning session, a new Sprint Backlog is created.

## Sprint Backlog Anti-Patterns

(aka Avoid Doing These)

#### Pre-assignment

When the Sprint Backlog is created during Sprint Planning, some teams decide who will work on which PBI or task. When it's kept to only one item, this isn't bad, however when all items are pre-assigned to team members, we have just planned for the first bottleneck.

#### One Person Doing Many Things

This happens when Team Members are signed up for one than one task or PBI at the same time. We can't multitask like we think we can because our brains just haven't evolved to do this. The more we multitask, the less we get done overall. So when Team Members sign up for more than one task at a time, they're promising to get less done. _Exception: if a team member has one item stuck in Blocked (or Waiting for), they might start work on another. If it happens again, the team should look into why one person's work is so frequently blocked. Alternative: when a team member has a item blocked, they might pair with another team member to help that person through the item._

#### Reporting

The Sprint Backlog loses its value if used for external purposes like reporting, or for [micro-management](/blog/scrum-anti-patterns-micromanagement/). When leadership uses it to look over the shoulders of the people doing the work — even if it's not to direct the Development Team's actions — it often leads to overloading the Sprint Backlog with details that undermine and eliminate transparency. The Sprint Backlog is used only by the Scrum team, and is not intended to be viewed by anyone else.

#### Multiple Sprints

Since Scrum is about adapting to the evolving work, it is pointless to plan which items will go into the Sprint Backlog beyond the current Sprint, so we shouldn't try to create Sprint Backlogs in advance. _I think this happens because some of the popular electronic tools make it possible and people assume, based on the tool, that this is a good practice._ Planning future Sprints before they happen reduces flexibility and increases workload for all involved. For a related rant on why adopting the tool doesn't make an organization Agile, see [JIRA is Not Agile](/blog/jira-is-not-agile/).

#### Phases

When people come from a traditional world into Scrum, some try to use the Sprint Backlog as a tool to recreate the phases they're used to. For example, they create columns in their Sprint Backlog for Analysis; Design; Development; Test. _While strictly speaking legal, they're recreating the boundaries between traditional roles, making collaboration less likely and ensuring handoffs between team members. As mentioned in the Limiting WIP segment, effective Teams work collaboratively through the Sprint to get a PBI to complete before moving onto the next. These phases tend to lead to another Scrum sin – Staggered Sprints._

## Forecasting with the Sprint Backlog

The Sprint Backlog is also the Developers' forecasting tool. Each day during [Daily Scrum](/blog/modern-guide-to-daily-scrum-meeting/), they replan their work and update the Sprint Backlog , using it to help them assess whether they're on track to meet their Sprint Goal. If they realize that their Sprint Goal is in jeopardy, they work with the Product Owner on replanning.

In the past, Teams used to use a [Sprint Burndown Chart](/blog/scrummaster-tales-the-trouble-with-sprint-burndowns/) that tracked task hours remaining to be done. Now, most of us would suggest that the focus on Tasks, versus focusing on User Stories/PBIs, is anti-pattern so we don't recommend Sprint Burndowns.

## Sprint Backlog vs Kanban Wall vs Product Backlog

While the Sprint Backlog is the Team's plan for the Sprint, the Product Backlog is the Teams queue of work. So the funny thing is that the Sprint Backlog and Product Backlog have easily confused names, but vastly different meanings. In my [workshops](/choose-the-right-scrum-training-for-your-needs/), whenever an attendee answers a question with, "Backlog", my instant response is, "Which one?"

A Sprint Backlog is far more like the (better-named) Kanban board. A Kanban board is a visual control system from the world of Kanban. It combines the Product Backlog with the Sprint Backlog. The key difference between Scrum's Sprint backlog and Kanban's board is that Kanban has a Work In Progess Limit. As you've already seen, I strongly recommend Scrum Teams steal a leaf from the Kanban world and do this.

## Key Points on Sprint Backlogs:

- Created by the Scrum Team
- An output of Sprint Planning
- Updated by the Scrum Team often during Daily Scrum
- Is better at progress tracking and forecasting than the Sprint Burndown
- Is used by team members to foster collaboration
- Contains whatever the team find useful - often includes the Sprint Goal and Improvements
- Tracks impediments, blockages, interruptions, [production support](/blog/scrum-production-support/) issues and hidden work
- A great data source to use for your next retrospective

Good Scrum teams know that they own the Sprint Backlog. _Great_ teams experiment every few Sprints to find what they can do to make their Sprint Backlog even better.

### Still Unsure How to Create an Effective Sprint Backlog?

Consider attending one of our [Certified ScrumMaster workshops](/courses/certified-scrummaster-csm-training/), where we discuss the _how_ and _why_ of Scrum, not just the _what_.  You'll get hands-on practical experience, and learn about some of the challenges – and solutions – along with tips on how to help your Team learn and grow to realize their potential.

[^1]: [Scrum Guide on Sprint Backlog](https://scrumguides.org/scrum-guide.html#sprint-backlog)

[^2]: This term describes work done out of sight of the team. It is also sometimes referred to as "dark work" (as in done in the dark), but "Hidden" or "Ghost" work is more culturally sensitive.

[^3]: This isn't a hard and fast rule. Instead, it's a pattern. As ScrumMaster or Agile Coach, if you see that the board is hinting at a problem, use that hint and look further to understand what is going on.

[^4]: [Github did a Developer Good Day survey and discovered that the more meetings someone is involved with, the less work they get done.](https://github.blog/2021-05-25-octoverse-spotlight-good-day-project/) My strong recommendation is that your only meeting most days should be Daily Scrum.

[^5]: These are called Niko Niko boards and not everyone thinks that they're a good idea.

17	
18	We're losing skills because we don't use them, and we're not growing the developers of the future. What do we give up to LLMs?
19	
20	When you use an LLM to make a decision you could make without the LLM, you gain a sense of false confidence. The easier it is to prompt an LLM to produce an answer, the less we develop the skill. This affects junior people more than senior people, since they have less overall experience to base their skills on.
21	
22	In the academic literature, this is called Deskilling. In radiology, AI assistants help detect abnormalities in medical images. In theory, these detect problems faster and don’t get tired. (In practice, there are open questions about their effectiveness.) Too much reliance on AI leaves the radiologist unable to detect on their own. Bad enough for the senior radiologists, but even worse for new doctors. When the AI Assistant was used in the learning process, the new doctor didn't have as deep an understanding of what they were seeing.
23	
24	This is a knowledge cliff, and the software industry is headed to one. (Hat tip to Brian Graham for the term.)
25	
26	NASA has been through this recently; they want to build big rockets again. They have mountains of documentation (literally 2900 cubic feet), but they don't have the understanding and tacit knowledge to use it.
27	
28	## Effects of Deskilling
29	- **Team Impact**: Reduced mentorship and knowledge sharing.
30	- **Long-Term Risk**: Novel or unexpected problems can't easily be solved with AI, leaving people unprepared.
31	- **Cognitive Atrophy**: Over-reliance on GenAI increases confidence in the AI while diminishing critical thinking skills.
32	
33	<Figure
34	  src={DeskillingCLD}
35	  alt="Causal loop diagram showing how LLM Reliance reduces Skill Practice, which reduces Developer Skill and Tacit Knowledge, ultimately diminishing the Ability to Solve Novel Problems, which in turn increases LLM Reliance"
36	  caption="Deskilling Causal Loop Diagram"
37	/>
38	
39	Brian Graham offers a question list: before automating with AI, ask:
40	- **Knowledge assessment** - do we understand the domain well enough to evaluate the AI output?
41	- Is this a **Core competency** vs **Background noise**?
42	- **Failure Planning** - Are we monitoring and prepared to reverse course if this decision fails?
43	
44	The more we use AI, the more critical thinking becomes important.
45	
46	Pilots have been through this before. With the advent of autopilot, instrument landing systems, automated flight management systems, etc., these systems have reduced the need for certain piloting skills. To combat this, they have increased the amount of training and simulator time for pilots to maintain their certifications.
47	
48	*I did not mention the 2026 Anthropic study: "How AI assistance impacts the formation of coding skills", because there are enough questions about the design and methodology that I don’t see it as a reliable source.*
49	
50	Deskilling and knowledge cliffs are a full module of our [Surviving the AI Tsunami course](/surviving-the-ai-tsunami-an-evidenced-based-course/), an evidence-based, cohort-based course for Agile teams.

---
title: 'AI and Skill Atrophy - Anti-Pattern'
date: '2026-02-24'
lastUpdated: '2026-02-24'
relatedTerms:
  - 'anti-patterns'
  - 'cross-skilling'
  - 'systems-thinking'
  - 'feature-factory'
excerpt: "Software's knowledge cliff: GenAI reliance erodes skills we don't practice. Juniors hit hardest with false confidence. Radiology detection fails without AI; NASA docs but no understanding."
---

import Figure from '@/components/global/figure.astro';
import HighlightBox from '@/components/global/highlight-box.astro';
import LinkList from '@/components/global/link-list.astro';
import DeskillingCLD from '@/content/glossary/ai-skill-atrophy/images/deskilling-cld.png';

We're losing skills because we don't use them, and we're not growing the developers of the future. What do we give up to LLMs?

When you use an LLM to make a decision you could make without the LLM, you gain a sense of false confidence. The easier it is to prompt an LLM to produce an answer, the less we develop the skill. This affects junior people more than senior people, since they have less overall experience to base their skills on.

In the academic literature, this is called Deskilling. In radiology, AI assistants help detect abnormalities in medical images. In theory, these detect problems faster and don’t get tired. (In practice, there are open questions about their effectiveness.) Too much reliance on AI leaves the radiologist unable to detect on their own. Bad enough for the senior radiologists, but even worse for new doctors. When the AI Assistant was used in the learning process, the new doctor didn't have as deep an understanding of what they were seeing.

This is a knowledge cliff, and the software industry is headed to one. (Hat tip to Brian Graham for the term.)

NASA has been through this recently; they want to build big rockets again. They have mountains of documentation (literally 2900 cubic feet), but they don't have the understanding and tacit knowledge to use it.

## Effects of Deskilling
- **Team Impact**: Reduced mentorship and knowledge sharing.
- **Long-Term Risk**: Novel or unexpected problems can't easily be solved with AI, leaving people unprepared.
- **Cognitive Atrophy**: Over-reliance on GenAI increases confidence in the AI while diminishing critical thinking skills.

<Figure
  src={DeskillingCLD}
  alt="Causal loop diagram showing how LLM Reliance reduces Skill Practice, which reduces Developer Skill and Tacit Knowledge, ultimately diminishing the Ability to Solve Novel Problems, which in turn increases LLM Reliance"
  caption="Deskilling Causal Loop Diagram"
/>

Brian Graham offers a question list: before automating with AI, ask:
- **Knowledge assessment** - do we understand the domain well enough to evaluate the AI output?
- Is this a **Core competency** vs **Background noise**?
- **Failure Planning** - Are we monitoring and prepared to reverse course if this decision fails?

The more we use AI, the more critical thinking becomes important.

Pilots have been through this before. With the advent of autopilot, instrument landing systems, automated flight management systems, etc., these systems have reduced the need for certain piloting skills. To combat this, they have increased the amount of training and simulator time for pilots to maintain their certifications.

*I did not mention the 2026 Anthropic study: "How AI assistance impacts the formation of coding skills", because there are enough questions about the design and methodology that I don’t see it as a reliable source.*

Deskilling and knowledge cliffs are a full module of our [Surviving the AI Tsunami course](/surviving-the-ai-tsunami-an-evidenced-based-course/), an evidence-based, cohort-based course for Agile teams.

2	title: 'Definition of Done'
3	date: '2023-11-29'
4	lastUpdated: '2026-03-03'
5	excerpt: 'Definition of Done is the team-created checklist that sets minimum quality for Scrum deliverables. It grounds Sprint Planning in real commitments and helps teams resist pressure to skip steps.'
6	relatedTerms: ['acceptance-criteria', 'agile-documentation', 'definition-of-ready', 'devops', 'sprint-goal', 'user-story']
7	---
8	
9	import Figure from '@/components/global/figure.astro';
10	import UnDoneAndDone from '@/content/glossary/definition-of-done/images/Un-Done-and-Done.jpg';
11	import APRBlogIllustrationsNov2019AcceptanceCriteriaAV21024x607 from '@/content/glossary/definition-of-done/images/APR_Blog-Illustrations_Nov2019_AcceptanceCriteria_A_v2-1024x607.jpg';
12	import LinkList from '@/components/global/link-list.astro';
13	import HighlightBox from '@/components/global/highlight-box.astro';
14	
15	**Definition of Done** is the official checklist that Scrum Teams maintain of the qualities they intend their work to achieve. It helps the team assess whether their work is truly completed and deliverable to the client as having added value. It also helps them in Sprint Planning by reminding them of the quality they have committed to achieving, ensuring they only commit to Product Backlog Items (PBIs) that they can get to truly “Done.”
16	
17	The Definition of Done serves as a common understanding with the whole Scrum team (including the Product Owner) about the quality of the product. When a team has a rigorous Definition of Done, the Product Owner should be able to release a new version of the product at the end of every Sprint.
18	
19	The 2020 Scrum Guide elevated Definition of Done to a formal "commitment" for the Increment, alongside Sprint Goal (for the Sprint Backlog) and Product Goal (for the Product Backlog). This framing reinforces that Done is not optional: it is the team's promise about what "complete" means.
20	
21	## How is Definition of Done different from Acceptance Criteria?
22	
23	Definition of Done is the universal checklist that all product backlog items are checked against. Being universal also makes it more generic. Acceptance Criteria are the specific details that are unique to that individual Product Backlog Item. An example will make this easier to understand. With a software development team, Done might include:
24	
25	- Unit test written for new code
26	- All Code Peer reviewed or Pair Programmed
27	- Acceptance Tests automated
28	- Usability Tests run
29	- Security Review complete
30	- …
31	
32	For a marketing team creating a website, Done might include:
33	
34	- Page has one H1 tag and three to four H2 tags
35	- Two pictures in the webp format and the pictures smaller than 50kb each
36	- Pictures have alt text
37	- All links on the page have been tested and link to the intended pages
38	- …
39	
40	## How is Definition of Done different from Definition of Ready?
41	
42	Definition of Ready describes the state a Product Backlog Item needs to be in *before* the team brings it into a Sprint. Definition of Done describes the qualities the work must have *after* the team completes it. Think of Ready as the entry gate and Done as the exit gate.
43	
44	One important distinction: Definition of Done is a core part of the Scrum framework. Definition of Ready is not part of the framework and should be used with caution. A rigid Definition of Ready can become a bottleneck, holding up work while requirements are perfected. If your team uses one, hold it lightly and keep it thin. See the [Definition of Ready](/glossary/definition-of-ready/) entry for a deeper look at the trade-offs.
45	
46	## Key Characteristics of the Definition of Done
47	
48	- **Clear and Specific** – any team member can read the list and understand what they mean. _Not every team member will be able to do all the work promised by Done._
49	- **Created by the whole Scrum Team** – all teams including the Product Owner and the ScrumMaster are involved in creating Done. _Hint: people won’t commit to something if they didn’t have a role in defining it._
50	- **Testable** – the team should understand how to test or prove each item
51	- **Minimum Quality** – Done sets the level of quality the team is promising to meet or exceed.
52	
53	## Steps to Defining "Done"
54	
55	This is just one exercise you can use to come up with an initial definition of “Done”. It is structured to ensure that the voices of all team members are heard.
56	
57	1. The Product Owner lays out their high-level needs. Remember, focus on qualities (e.g. no memory leaks) and not business needs.
58	2. Working in small groups, (e.g. 2-3) team members brainstorm the individual elements required to meet those needs, (e.g. Load Tests run) and other things they judge necessary, (e.g. Unit Testing).
59	3. Combine the exact matches and similar items. Find the outliers. Group work/Silent sort – best done with the most senior people going last and not first.
60	4. Eliminate suggestions that the group feels don’t make sense.
61	5. Team members decide on their own how frequently each element of “Done” can be met per: Story, Sprint or Release – as it stands today. There is a strong preference to get truly “Done” every Sprint. However at first some teams won’t.
62	6. Team members vote/agree on where items fit today, (e.g. Story/Sprint/Release).
63	
64	At this stage we post the list on the Task/Story wall. Often the team adjust their columns on the wall to match the “Done” criteria.
65	
66	If the team decided on “Undone” work (e.g. work delayed until Hardening Sprint), then they need to make that clear as well. They then need to clear a plan to ensure that they eliminate the Hardening Sprint over time.
67	
68	## Improving the Definition of Done Over Time
69	
70	One area of misunderstanding is that some team members expect that Done changes every Sprint. If that happened, the product’s quality would be very inconsistent. Imagine if one Sprint the team released features with Automated Acceptance tests, and the next Sprint they don’t even have Unit Tests. Scrum Teams should have the same Definition of Done, Sprint over Sprint. This gives the Product Owner consistent expectations around quality. As a team becomes more skilled and automates some steps in Done, then they should make their Done stronger or more rigorous. While this takes time, the increase in rigour will reduce the number of defects in the long run.
71	
72	## Impediments or Problems in Achieving Done
73	
74	When a team is new, they find it hard to achieve Done. As a result, the Product Owner can’t be sure if it is okay to ship the product. Many of these problems are from lack of skill or knowledge in something that affects Done. In our software team example, the team might have limited knowledge around Automating Acceptance Tests. Our marketing team might lack the graphics design skill to produce their own images. Cross-skilling and pairing (with someone outside the team) are going to be the approaches that help the team grow until they always produce a releasable product.
75	
76	The other problem to achieving Done is pressure to deliver more features (or User Stories). As the pressure builds, the team may respond by compromising on Done. In the short term this appears to be fine, as they appear to get more work finished. In the long run, the increase in bugs inevitably offsets the value of the added work. Each shortcut accumulates as [technical debt](/blog/scrummaster-tales-technical-debt-is-slowing-the-team/), making future work slower and more error-prone.
77	
78	Trying to stuff more work into the pipeline always fails. Instead of more work, the organization needs to a better job deciding which Product Backlog Items will deliver the most value and prioritize those. The Team themselves need to start Sprint Planning with a clear understanding of their own Definition of Done. During Sprint Planning, they only take on work that they can bring to truly Done.
79	
80	## Undone Work
81	
82	<Figure
83	  src={UnDoneAndDone}
84	  alt="Undone work vs Truly Done in Scrum"
85	  caption="Undone work vs Truly Done in Scrum"
86	/>
87	
88	
89	When a product is not truly releasable at the end of Sprint, the difference is often referred to as Undone work. Why is this a problem? It’s a problem because it reduced transparency. The Product Owner and clients think the team have completed work on those User Stories. Yet the work isn’t complete. Here are a few examples of how the work that looks finished, but doesn’t meet the Definition of Done, becomes a problem later:
90	
91	- A bug is found several Sprints after the code is written and now new code relies on the defective behaviour.
92	- Missing a security audit, the application is susceptible to a SQL injection attack.
93	- Missing a usability review, the new User stories are difficult for the client to use (e.g. colour blindness, …)
94	- The Application is deployed and doesn’t work with the current firewall configuration.
95	
96	**Non-Software Examples:**
97	
98	- Lacking alt text, pictures displayed on a page are undetectable to blind users.
99	- Large pictures mean the page takes longer to load and clients abandon the site because they’re bored of waiting.
100	
101	Scrum expects that, at a minimum, the product be “Potentially Releasable” at the end of Sprint. This reduces risk and allows the Product Owner and the client to have confidence that  User Stories the team claim to have Done, are truly Done.
102	
103	## Limitations of Done
104	
105	The team need to be honest about what is Done and what is not really done. The bigger challenge is for teams that work on a variety of Products. For example, a non-software team that is doing marketing work might have a number of different work products: a website; videos; artwork; Google ads; Facebook ads; … . In this case, the Done will become very fragmented and will be harder to use. But Done is perhaps even more important in these cases because it acts as a reminder for someone who less familiar with the work of all the things that need to be completed to deliver high quality.
106	
107	### Can Done be used as an auditable checklist for reporting?
108	
109	_Eewww._ This sounds very traditional. I only include this because I’ve seen this with clients and we need to stamp it out. Definition of Done is for the Scrum Team to understand the quality of the product they’re creating. It’s not a reporting standard. From the teams I’ve heard from, using it as a reporting standard leads to micro management. Someone reads or hears a report related to Done and asks the team to stop doing some aspect of Done, so they can produce more User Stories. As shown above, this always leads to an increase in defects weeks or months after the initial decision was made.

112	  src={APRBlogIllustrationsNov2019AcceptanceCriteriaAV21024x607}
113	  alt="Definition of Done vs. User Stories vs. Acceptance Criteria - image by Agile Pain Relief Consulting"
114	  caption="Definition of Done vs. User Stories vs. Acceptance Criteria - image by Agile Pain Relief Consulting"
115	/>

subject: 'Are You Planning Enough? (Spoiler: Probably Not)'

Hi {{ subscriber.first_name }}, 
Timing is everything. Just before disappearing on vacation, I asked for your help naming what I'm doing with GenAI. 

Am I acting as a:
🗺️ AI Cartographer - mapping the terrain, cliffs and all 
🏔️ AI Sherpa - trusted guide through difficult, uncertain territory 
📐 AI Surveyor - measuring what is really on the ground

I got some great feedback, and I'm still digesting it all. I even got a write-in candidate: AI Pathfinder - because I'm helping find the path through rocky terrain. Doing this right before a vacation may not have been my brightest move.

So what do you think - which label fits best?
## Intentional
I travelled to the Canary Islands for a hiking vacation. On the Island of La Gomera, I experienced [Storm "Therese](https://lagomera1.blogspot.com/2026/03/la-gomera-hit-by-storms-torrential-rain.html)". Hiking got replaced by reflection and reading more of [Chris Bailey's book: "Intentional: How to Finish What You Start"](https://www.amazon.ca/Intentional-How-Finish-What-Start/dp/1039011608/ref=sr_1_1?crid=3PAS3E9MMIJSK&dib=eyJ2IjoiMSJ9.6bbqAWns9DH4qy97NTKbr0uaVrrK7wWxnu7IEn2rRxI.foN2UrwRvkBVjvzc2RS1-HNZY6Fg_sASA-Svcnn5i08&dib_tag=se&keywords=intentional+chris+bailey&qid=1775144954&sprefix=chris+bai%2Caps%2C210&sr=8-1). I thought I was reading this only for me. Now, as I look back, I realize the book has value for Agile teams. By default, as humans we spend about 5% of our time planning and 95% implementing those plans. (I don't even think I hit 5%.) The research suggests that the number should be closer to 20% planning and 80% action. In the book, he shows that goal attainment happens in part because we plan on many levels, from life goals, all the way down to what is the best thing I should do today.

Thinking about Scrum, all of Sprint Planning, Review, Retrospective, and Daily Scrum are about planning and goal attainment. Officially, they're supposed to occupy 10% of the Sprint. We also have Backlog Refinement, which, based on experience, takes up another 3-5% of a Sprint. Scrum anticipated the research that Chris found for his book by more than a decade.

When we see teams first adopt Scrum, there is often pushback: too much time spent on planning and not enough time doing. I've always known the pushback was misplaced and now I have research to support it.

If you want to make Backlog Refinement better for your team, look at: [Product Backlog Refinement Hell: 3 Problems and Solutions](https://agilepainrelief.com/blog/product-backlog-refinement-hell-solutions/)

As we move into a world where GenAI can help us do some of the heavy lifting, intentions and planning will be ever more important. Shipping unproven features faster is not winning. Yet many teams are using GenAI to rip through their Product Backlog without considering whether the work has any value.

To thrive in this new world, we will need better Product Ownership and Quality.
## Ottawa Product Camp 2026
If you want to hone your Product Ownership skills and meet with other professionals, join me on April 18th for Ottawa Product Camp. It's an unconference where the audience selects the sessions. From the description: "This event is for anyone involved or interested in managing, marketing, developing, building, and/or scaling a product. Whether you are curious to learn more about product management & marketing or want to accelerate your career and expand your knowledge, this is a great opportunity to learn and network in a collaborative, fun, informal and supportive environment."

[https://www.ottawapmma.ca](https://www.ottawapmma.ca/productcampottawa) -- if you scroll down you can see the sessions proposed thus far. I've proposed one session: "Where Do Product Managers need to go to survive AI?"

Once you have signed up, you can also propose a session: 
https://docs.google.com/forms/d/e/1FAIpQLSfGd8aQJI13Ed90e8f2ZZtVRbWcR5ZJAFL7GvK_I0vzA641DQ/viewform

In the days before the event, we will vote on which sessions will be held. 

## Quality
If GenAI needs better Product Management, it also needs a real emphasis on Quality. You used Lean Startup to run experiments and validated the feature. Awesome. Now we need to work on quality. Back by popular demand [Certified Scrum Developer Workshop](https://agilepainrelief.corsizio.com/event/69cd8ce7066b8e5ce999e15d).  - June 22 - 25, 12:30 pm - 5:00 pm Eastern time. Along with quality, we also tackle what it takes to build productive teams. As long as humans are doing work, we will need teams. This isn't going away.

Cheers
Mark

P.S. Take some time to look at the leaked portion of Claude Code. Many people have commented on hidden features (meh), how much you have to beg an LLM to behave (not surprised). I'm shocked at the quality and the volume of duplication. Print.ts has a single function over 3000 lines with 12 levels of nesting. This isn't maintainable. The situation is so bad that if you work for Anthropic, I will offer a discount on my upcoming [CSD workshop](https://agilepainrelief.corsizio.com/event/69cd8ce7066b8e5ce999e15d).

# Social posts — week of 2026-07-14 (next-few-days batch)

Working draft. Five items pulled from `complete-social-media-calendar.md`: 2 blog posts, 2 glossary entries, 1 older newsletter. **Each has two draft options (A/B) - pick one per item, tweak in your own voice, then tell me and I'll build the 3-platform batch JSON** at `analytics/social-media-content-evergreen/next-few-days.json`, condensing each to LinkedIn / Mastodon (<=500) / Bluesky (<=290).

Drafts lean on your own words from the source posts. GenAI items hold the glass-1/3-full line.

Conventions when I build the JSON: the URL goes in the `url` field (no UTM, no inline links; the pipeline adds per-platform UTM), and `image` stays `""` (the pipeline scrapes og:image).

**Selection (all `[ ]` in the queue):**
- Blog — GenAI Code Quality: Fundamental Flaws and Bluffing (TIER 1, top of queue)
- Blog — The Sprint Backlog: Complete Guide (TIER 2)
- Glossary — AI and Skill Atrophy (TIER 1)
- Glossary — Definition of Done
- Newsletter — "Are You Planning Enough?" (2026-04-02)

---

## 1. Blog — GenAI code quality / bluffing (glass 1/3 full)
**URL:** /blog/genai-code-quality-fundamental-flaws-and-how-bluffing-makes-it-worse/

### Option A — the data
AI-generated code has 1.7x more issues, and the quality gap is turning into a chasm.

That's not a random number. It's from a CodeRabbit research report: 30-41% more tech debt, 39% more cognitive complexity. And the flaws are structural. Training rewards code that compiles and passes tests. There's no reward for code that's easy to maintain, so the model optimises for "does it work" and nothing else.

You can't code review your way out of that. That just puts the burden on humans to tidy up the mess the model made.

I use these tools daily. The fix isn't more speed: give the model smaller, more focused tasks, and make sure you know what the right product is first.

#AIinSoftwareDevelopment

### Option B — the bluffing
GenAI doesn't write bad code because it's dumb. It writes bad code because of how it's rewarded.

Training and evaluation reward code that compiles and passes the tests. 0-1 grading schemes reward guessing over admitting a lack of knowledge, so the model learns to bluff: plausible, overconfident best guesses. OX Security calls it an army of junior developers, fast and functional, but lacking architectural judgment.

TDD helps. Code review helps. Neither fixes a structural problem baked in at training time.

Genuinely useful for the dull work, oversold on the rest. Knowing where GenAI erodes quality is how you use it well.

#AIinSoftwareDevelopment #Agile

---

## 2. Blog — Sprint Backlog
**URL:** /blog/the-humble-sprint-backlog/

### Option A — ownership
If your Sprint Backlog is whatever your online tool feeds you, it isn't really yours.

The Sprint Backlog is created by the Team, for the Team. When you just accept what the tool spits out, it reinforces the sense that Scrum is happening to them, not something they choose. That quietly kills engagement.

Good Scrum teams know they own the Sprint Backlog. Great teams experiment every few Sprints to make it better: steal a WIP limit from Kanban, add an interruptions lane, pin the Sprint Goal at the top.

Own it first. Then improve it.

#Scrum #ScrumMaster

### Option B — anti-pattern
The fastest way to hobble a Sprint Backlog: pre-assign every item on day one.

When all items are pre-assigned to team members, you've just planned for the first bottleneck. Same story when it becomes a reporting tool and leadership starts looking over shoulders. It loses its value.

The Sprint Backlog is a plan by and for the Developers. It's used only by the Scrum Team, not as a status report for anyone else.

Keep it the team's. Limit WIP. Let people pull the work they're ready for.

#Scrum #ProductOwner

---

## 3. Glossary — AI and Skill Atrophy (glass 1/3 full)
**URL:** /glossary/ai-skill-atrophy/

### Option A — the knowledge cliff
NASA wants to build big rockets again. They have 2,900 cubic feet of documentation and not enough people who still understand it.

That's a knowledge cliff, and the software industry is walking toward one. When you use an LLM to make a decision you could have made yourself, you gain false confidence and lose a little skill. It hits juniors hardest, because they have less experience to fall back on. Radiologists who lean too hard on AI detection struggle to spot problems on their own.

Before you automate with GenAI, ask: do we understand this well enough to judge the output? The more we use AI, the more critical thinking matters.

#AIinSoftwareDevelopment #Leadership

### Option B — the pilots
We're losing skills because we don't use them.

The easier it is to prompt an LLM for an answer, the less we build the skill ourselves. Academics call it deskilling. Pilots hit this decades ago with autopilot, and their fix was more training and simulator time, not less. Software is walking into the same trap, except we're cutting practice instead of protecting it.

GenAI is genuinely useful for the dull work. Just don't let it quietly take the practice your juniors need to become seniors.

#AIinSoftwareDevelopment

---

## 4. Glossary — Definition of Done
**URL:** /glossary/definition-of-done/

### Option A — the pressure
The moment the pressure builds, most teams quietly negotiate their Definition of Done downward.

In the short term it looks fine: more stories finished. In the long run the bugs offset the value, and each shortcut accumulates as technical debt that makes future work slower and more error-prone.

Done is not optional. It's the team's promise about what "complete" actually means. Work that looks finished but doesn't meet Done hasn't saved you time, it's just hidden the cost.

Only take on work in Sprint Planning that you can bring to truly Done.

#Scrum #ScrumMaster

### Option B — undone work
"Done" and "looks done" are not the same thing, and the gap has a name: Undone work.

The Product Owner thinks the story shipped. It didn't. A bug surfaces three Sprints later and new code already relies on the broken behaviour. Skip the security review and hello, SQL injection. Undone work reduces transparency, and that's the real damage.

A rigorous Definition of Done is what lets the Product Owner release at the end of every Sprint with confidence. And it's for the team, not a reporting standard. Use it to report upward and you just breed micromanagement.

#Scrum #ProductOwner

---

## 5. Newsletter — "Are You Planning Enough?" (2026-04-02)
**URL:** /newsletter-subscribe/
*(Newsletters aren't published as individual pages, so this drives to signup. Swap in a web-archive link if you'd rather point at the issue itself.)*

### Option A — the 5% vs 20%
By default, we humans spend about 5% of our time planning and 95% doing. The research says it should be closer to 20% planning, 80% action.

I found that in Chris Bailey's book Intentional, on a hiking trip that turned into a reading trip when a storm rolled in. Then it clicked: Scrum anticipated this by more than a decade. Sprint Planning, Review, Retrospective, Daily Scrum, plus Backlog Refinement land around 13-15% of a Sprint spent on planning and goal attainment.

The usual pushback when teams adopt Scrum is "too much planning, not enough doing." Turns out that pushback is misplaced, and now there's research to back it up.

#Scrum #Agile

### Option B — planning in a GenAI world
Many teams are using GenAI to rip through their Product Backlog without ever asking whether the work has any value.

Shipping unproven features faster is not winning. We default to about 5% planning and 95% doing, when the research points closer to 20% planning as where goals actually get met. Scrum already builds that in: Planning, Review, Retro, Daily Scrum, Refinement.

To thrive in a world where GenAI does more of the heavy lifting, we'll need better Product Ownership and quality, not just more output. Spend the 20%. Decide what's worth building before you let the machine build it.

#AIinSoftwareDevelopment #ProductOwner

120	## Mark's Voice Profile (applies to all LinkedIn posts)
121	
122	### Core Tone
123	- Conversational yet professional. Like coworkers talking at a pub after work.
124	- First person singular for observations ("I've seen...", "In my experience...").
125	- First person plural for solutions ("We can improve...", "What if we...").
126	- Direct address to reader ("you", "your team").
127	- Contractions used naturally.
128	- Confident without arrogance. Educational. Empathetic to practitioner reality.
129	- Canadian English spelling (behaviour, colour, organisation) preferred.
130	
131	### Signature Patterns (SHOULD appear, when appropriate)
132	- Parenthetical asides for clarification, humour, or Scrum reminders.
133	- Self-deprecating humour, especially about estimation, being a "recovering programmer", or
134	  feeling old.
135	- Grounding abstract points in practitioner reality: "Teams I work with...", "I've seen...".
136	- Cites evidence (studies, DORA, named research) when making claims.
137	
138	### Anti-Patterns (should NOT appear)
139	
140	#### Buzzwords & Corporate Speak -- REJECT
141	- "Delve" (hard rule -- Mark never uses this word)
142	- "Unlock", "Unleash", "Elevate", "Supercharge", "Revolutionize", "Transform your..."
143	- "Game-changer", "Best-in-class", "Cutting-edge", "State-of-the-art", "Next-level"
144	- "Synergy", "Leverage" (verb), "Optimize" (vague), "Disrupt/Disruptive"
145	- "Rockstar", "Ninja", "Guru", "Badass" (applied to people)
146	- "Deep dive", "Unpack" (both overused)
147	- "Journey" (corporate metaphor), "Ecosystem", "Paradigm shift"
148	- "Move the needle", "Circle back", "Low-hanging fruit", "Boil the ocean"
149	- "Stakeholder alignment" -> "getting everyone on the same page"
150	
151	#### Punctuation & Formatting
152	- No emdash (-- ). Mark uses hyphens surrounded by spaces instead. Hard rule.
153	- Excessive exclamation points. One per post at most.
154	- Generic LLM-style openers: "Moreover", "Furthermore", "In conclusion", "It's worth noting that".
155	- Every paragraph starting the same way.
156	
157	#### LLM Rhetorical Tells -- REJECT
158	These are the giveaways that a post was drafted or polished by an LLM. Flag them hard.
159	
160	- **Contrast-framing overload ("not X, it's Y").** AI loves the negation-then-correction
161	  flip: "The goal isn't to use GenAI more, or less. It's to lead a team that uses it well."
162	  "Marketing isn't about selling, it's about connecting." "Success isn't luck, it's
163	  preparation." Humans don't speak in constant opposites. One earned contrast in a post is
164	  fine; a rhythm of them reads as manufactured insight. Say the positive claim directly, or
165	  back the contrast with something concrete instead of a rhetorical flip. Watch the sibling
166	  move too: "I'm not X, I'm Y" self-positioning ("I'm not there as a guru, I'm the guide who...").
167	- **The manufactured-vulnerability beat.** "I teach this for a living, I was being careful,
168	  and I still missed it." The confess-a-flaw-then-pivot-to-authority move. It signals humility
169	  while actually reasserting expertise, and readers now recognise it as a template. If Mark is
170	  sharing a real mistake, let it sit as a real mistake without the redemptive turn that
171	  converts it back into a credential.
172	- **Cringe transition questions.** "The catch?" "The kicker?" "The brutal truth?" AI treats
173	  these as engagement buttons; they read like infomercial patter ("But wait, there's more!").
174	  Cut them and let the next sentence stand on its own.
175	- **Tricolon build-ups.** "Knowing where it helps, where it quietly adds risk, and how to tell
176	  the difference." The rule-of-three cadence is a tell when every list snaps to exactly three
177	  parallel clauses. Vary the rhythm or make it two.
178	
179	#### Scrum Terminology -- USE THESE RULES
180	- "ScrumMaster" -- one word, capital S and M. Never "Scrum Master".
181	- "Sprint", "Product Backlog", "Product Owner", "Effective Scrum" -- all capitalised.
182	
183	#### AI / GenAI Terminology -- USE THESE RULES
184	- Say "GenAI" or "LLM" -- never bare "AI" when referring to generative tools. Bare "AI" is
185	  acceptable for artificial intelligence as a field.
186	- Never call LLMs "intelligent" -- they are tools, not minds.
187	- Never hype capabilities. Acknowledge limitations alongside benefits.
188	- Bottleneck framing: "Writing code was never the bottleneck."
189	
190	#### Tone Anti-Patterns
191	- Salesy or promotional ("Don't miss this amazing opportunity!").
192	- Arrogant expertise display ("As a leading expert..."). Demonstrate, don't claim.
193	- Apologetic hedging ("I think maybe perhaps...").
194	- Impersonal distance ("one might consider..."). Use "you" and "I".
195	
196	---
197	
198	## LinkedIn-Specific Conventions
199	
200	### Length
201	- 100-250 words typical. Punchy, one clear point per post. This is the default.
202	- Evidence note: the State of the Algorithm Q1 2026 report found longer posts (toward 1,500-3,000 characters, roughly 250-480 words) perform well on reach. Go longer when the topic has real depth and you can hold attention. Mark's own LinkedIn data says topic matters more than length, so don't pad a thin idea to hit a character count.
203	- Lead with the surprising data point, observation, or question. Don't bury the lead.
204	- Substance over padding.
205	
206	### Hook & Opening
207	Strong opening patterns (pick one, don't stack):
208	- **Research hook**: "New research reality check:", "Plot twist: [study] shows..."
209	- **Provocative statement**: A claim that makes the reader stop scrolling.
210	- **Rhetorical question**: One the reader has probably wondered about.
211	- **Personal observation**: "I've been watching teams...", "Something I keep seeing..."
212	
213	Flag weak openings: generic setup ("In today's world..."), throat-clearing, or
214	context that could be cut without losing meaning.
215	
216	### Body Structure
217	- One clear point. Resist cramming multiple arguments.
218	- Perception vs. reality gaps work well (what people believe vs. what evidence shows).
219	- Lists of 2-4 items are fine; longer lists dilute the post.
220	- Connect back to what matters -- healthy teams, good software, practitioner reality.
221	- Close with a practitioner takeaway when the topic warrants it: a single line that hands the reader an action, a question, or a frame to apply. Scrum and GenAI posts land harder with one. Personal and seasonal posts usually don't need it.
222	
223	### Emoji
224	- **Cross-platform now:** emoji are used on Mastodon and Bluesky too, not just LinkedIn. For pipeline (batch) posts, the shared `_social-posting-conventions.md` in the agile-pain-relief-astro repo is the source of truth (same 1-2 rule; on Bluesky they count against the 290-char limit). The LinkedIn-specific detail below applies to organic LinkedIn posts.
225	- Strategic, understated. Up to two emoji per post is fine; more is cluttered.
226	- Opening emoji to catch attention works. A second emoji can mark a structural turn (e.g., the constructive pivot after a critique).
227	- Why they help: LinkedIn body text is uniform grey, so a well-placed emoji adds colour, breaks up the text, and pulls the eye to a key point or the CTA. That is the mechanism behind the report's emoji finding; it does not license overuse.
228	- Never emoji a vulnerability beat or a serious moment - it undercuts the weight.
229	
230	### Hashtags
231	- Minimal. Often none. When used, keep to 1-3 and make them meaningful
232	  (e.g., #EffectiveScrum for Scrum posts). Avoid hashtag salad.
233	- Evidence: the Q1 2026 report found posts with more than 3 hashtags performed 71% worse than posts with none. The algorithm already reads your keywords, so extra hashtags add little and can signal a weaker creator.
234	
235	### Calls to Action
236	- Genuine engagement requests over performative ones ("Looking for anecdotes about..."
237	  beats "What do you think? Comment below!"). Generic "What do you think?" prompts are dead -
238	  use a genuine question or a provocative statement instead.
239	
240	### Links
241	- Put links in the post body, not in the comments. "Link in the comments" is the dead pattern.
242	- Links do not tank reach. The Q1 2026 report found posts with 1-3 links got 43% higher reach, and
243	  posts with more than 3 links got 441% higher reach, because link-heavy posts read as genuinely
244	  useful resource collections. Links to agilepainrelief.com are fine when the destination is genuinely useful.
245	- A natural fit for Mark: one link to his own article plus a few to the sources he footnoted.
246	- Quality bar: every link should be something the reader actually wants, not filler.
247	
248	---
249	
250	## Topic Modes (calibrate tone to the topic)
251	
252	Posts generally fall into one of these modes. The voice is consistent; the lean differs.
253	
254	### Scrum / Agile Practice
255	- **Tone**: Educational, helpful, empathetic to struggles.
256	- **Evidence**: Experience-based, practitioner stories, anti-patterns observed in the wild.
257	- **Goal**: Help readers fix problems in their teams.
258	- **Structure**: Often a problem + misdiagnosis + what actually works.
259	- **Hashtags**: Regular (e.g., #EffectiveScrum).
260	
261	### AI / GenAI / LLMs in Software and Scrum
262	- **Tone**: Skeptical pragmatist -- not anti-AI, not hype. Measured, analytical.
263	- **Evidence**: Research-and-data-based (e.g., the 19%/20% perception-gap study, DORA rollback
264	  signals). Cite specifics when possible.
265	- **Goal**: Question assumptions; surface hidden costs; ground hype in evidence.
266	- **Structure**: Provocative claim + counter-evidence + implication. "Hidden costs nobody talks
267	  about" framing works well. Always connect back to Scrum values (collaboration, human judgement,
268	  context over speed) when relevant.
269	- **Hashtags**: Minimal, sometimes none.
270	- **Watch for**: Drift into dismissive or mocking territory. Mark's position is "I'm not against
271	  GenAI, but let's be realistic." Acknowledge potential benefits before the "but".
272	
273	### Personal / Travel / Seasonal
274	- **Tone**: Warm, conversational, light. Pub-with-coworkers voice at its purest.
275	- **Evidence**: Not required; this is connective tissue.
276	- **Goal**: Build relationship with the audience.
277	- **Watch for**: Too-long personal posts that lose their thread. Brevity is kindness.
278	
279	### Workshop / Training / Business Announcements
280	- **Tone**: Direct, low-key. Inform, don't sell.
281	- **Watch for**: Salesy language, exclamation marks, "amazing opportunity" energy.
282	
283	If a post spans modes (common for AI-meets-Scrum posts), apply both rubrics.
284	
285	---
286	
287	## Critique Output Format
288	
289	Structure the response like this:
290	
291	### Overall Impression
292	[2-3 sentences: Does this land? What's the main issue?]
293	
294	### Voice & Tone
295	[Does this sound like Mark? Where does it, where doesn't it?]
296	
297	### Hook & Opening
298	[Is the first line doing enough work? Specific feedback.]
299	
300	### Structure & Length
301	[Length check, one-clear-point check, flow.]
302	
303	### Anti-Pattern Detections
304	For each:
305	> **Found**: "[exact quote]"
306	> **Issue**: [which anti-pattern, or why this grates]
307	> **Suggested fix**: "[rewritten phrase in Mark's voice]"
308	
309	### Terminology & Language
310	[Flag issues only: ScrumMaster spelling, GenAI/LLM usage, capitalisation, buzzwords, emdash. If the draft gets all of these right, omit this section - Mark knows his own rules and doesn't need praise for following them.]
311	
312	### Engagement Mechanics
313	[Emoji count and use, hashtag choice, CTA quality.]
314	
315	### Practitioner Takeaway
316	[Does the post hand the reader something they can do, think about, or test in their own work? Scrum and GenAI posts land harder with a closing line that gives the reader an action or a frame to apply. Not every post needs one - personal and seasonal posts rarely do - so flag only when one would clearly help, and don't force one where it doesn't fit.]
317	
318	### Strengths
319	[Specific phrases or moves that nail the voice. Be concrete.]
320	
321	### Priority Fixes
322	[Top 3-5 changes ranked by impact, with brief rationale. These should be the improvements
323	Mark would actually make before posting.]
324	
325	---
326	
327	## Reference Material
328	
329	- `APR/Efforts/Newsletter/` -- any newsletter file demonstrates Mark's voice at length.
330	  Good calibration if a draft feels off and you want to recalibrate before critiquing.
331	- `Skills/APR/newsletter-reviewer/SKILL.md` -- the longer-form sibling of this skill. Voice profile
332	  and anti-pattern list overlap; this skill is the LinkedIn-shaped subset.
333	- `OutsideContent/Generated/State of the LinkedIn Algorithm Q1 2026 - Report and Call Notes.md` --
334	  the evidence behind the length, links, hashtag, and emoji guidance here (Q1 2026 algorithm data plus
335	  Mike Schmitz's commentary). Read it if you want the numbers or to re-check a convention.
336	
337	---
338	
339	## Important Notes
340	
341	- Mark does all his own writing. This skill helps him sharpen drafts, not replace them.
342	- The goal is to help Mark sound more like himself. His quirks, self-deprecation, and
343	  practitioner-grounded examples are features, not bugs.
344	- When in doubt, lean toward "a knowledgeable friend at a pub" over "a consultant on a panel".
345	- Mark's LinkedIn audience is ScrumMasters, Agile Coaches, Product Owners, managers, and
346	  adjacent practitioners. They often know what to do but lack the influence to change it.
347	  Empathy for that tension matters.
