- "Synergy", "Leverage" (verb), "Optimize" (vague), "Disrupt/Disruptive"
- "Rockstar", "Ninja", "Guru", "Badass" (applied to people)
- "Deep dive", "Unpack" (both overused)
- "Journey" (corporate metaphor), "Ecosystem", "Paradigm shift"
- "Move the needle", "Circle back", "Low-hanging fruit", "Boil the ocean"
- "Stakeholder alignment" -> "getting everyone on the same page"

#### Punctuation & Formatting
- No emdash (-- ). Mark uses hyphens surrounded by spaces instead. Hard rule.
- Excessive exclamation points. One per post at most.
- Generic LLM-style openers: "Moreover", "Furthermore", "In conclusion", "It's worth noting that".
- Every paragraph starting the same way.

#### LLM Rhetorical Tells -- REJECT
These are the giveaways that a post was drafted or polished by an LLM. Flag them hard.

- **Contrast-framing overload ("not X, it's Y").** AI loves the negation-then-correction
  flip: "The goal isn't to use GenAI more, or less. It's to lead a team that uses it well."
  "Marketing isn't about selling, it's about connecting." "Success isn't luck, it's
  preparation." Humans don't speak in constant opposites. One earned contrast in a post is
  fine; a rhythm of them reads as manufactured insight. Say the positive claim directly, or
  back the contrast with something concrete instead of a rhetorical flip. Watch the sibling
  move too: "I'm not X, I'm Y" self-positioning ("I'm not there as a guru, I'm the guide who...").
- **The manufactured-vulnerability beat.** "I teach this for a living, I was being careful,
  and I still missed it." The confess-a-flaw-then-pivot-to-authority move. It signals humility
  while actually reasserting expertise, and readers now recognise it as a template. If Mark is
  sharing a real mistake, let it sit as a real mistake without the redemptive turn that
  converts it back into a credential.
- **Cringe transition questions.** "The catch?" "The kicker?" "The brutal truth?" AI treats
  these as engagement buttons; they read like infomercial patter ("But wait, there's more!").
  Cut them and let the next sentence stand on its own.
- **Tricolon build-ups.** "Knowing where it helps, where it quietly adds risk, and how to tell
  the difference." The rule-of-three cadence is a tell when every list snaps to exactly three
  parallel clauses. Vary the rhythm or make it two.

#### Scrum Terminology -- USE THESE RULES
- "ScrumMaster" -- one word, capital S and M. Never "Scrum Master".
- "Sprint", "Product Backlog", "Product Owner", "Effective Scrum" -- all capitalised.

#### AI / GenAI Terminology -- USE THESE RULES
- Say "GenAI" or "LLM" -- never bare "AI" when referring to generative tools. Bare "AI" is
  acceptable for artificial intelligence as a field.
- Never call LLMs "intelligent" -- they are tools, not minds.
- Never hype capabilities. Acknowledge limitations alongside benefits.
- Bottleneck framing: "Writing code was never the bottleneck."

#### Tone Anti-Patterns
- Salesy or promotional ("Don't miss this amazing opportunity!").
- Arrogant expertise display ("As a leading expert..."). Demonstrate, don't claim.
- Apologetic hedging ("I think maybe perhaps...").
- Impersonal distance ("one might consider..."). Use "you" and "I".

---

## LinkedIn-Specific Conventions

### Length
- 100-250 words typical. Punchy, one clear point per post. This is the default.
- Evidence note: the State of the Algorithm Q1 2026 report found longer posts (toward 1,500-3,000 characters, roughly 250-480 words) perform well on reach. Go longer when the topic has real depth and you can hold attention. Mark's own LinkedIn data says topic matters more than length, so don't pad a thin idea to hit a character count.
- Lead with the surprising data point, observation, or question. Don't bury the lead.
- Substance over padding.

### Hook & Opening
Strong opening patterns (pick one, don't stack):
- **Research hook**: "New research reality check:", "Plot twist: [study] shows..."
- **Provocative statement**: A claim that makes the reader stop scrolling.
- **Rhetorical question**: One the reader has probably wondered about.
- **Personal observation**: "I've been watching teams...", "Something I keep seeing..."

Flag weak openings: generic setup ("In today's world..."), throat-clearing, or
context that could be cut without losing meaning.

### Body Structure
- One clear point. Resist cramming multiple arguments.
- Perception vs. reality gaps work well (what people believe vs. what evidence shows).
- Lists of 2-4 items are fine; longer lists dilute the post.
- Connect back to what matters -- healthy teams, good software, practitioner reality.
- Close with a practitioner takeaway when the topic warrants it: a single line that hands the reader an action, a question, or a frame to apply. Scrum and GenAI posts land harder with one. Personal and seasonal posts usually don't need it.

### Emoji
- **Cross-platform now:** emoji are used on Mastodon and Bluesky too, not just LinkedIn. For pipeline (batch) posts, the shared `_social-posting-conventions.md` in the agile-pain-relief-astro repo is the source of truth (same 1-2 rule; on Bluesky they count against the 290-char limit). The LinkedIn-specific detail below applies to organic LinkedIn posts.
- Strategic, understated. Up to two emoji per post is fine; more is cluttered.
- Opening emoji to catch attention works. A second emoji can mark a structural turn (e.g., the constructive pivot after a critique).
- Why they help: LinkedIn body text is uniform grey, so a well-placed emoji adds colour, breaks up the text, and pulls the eye to a key point or the CTA. That is the mechanism behind the report's emoji finding; it does not license overuse.
- Never emoji a vulnerability beat or a serious moment - it undercuts the weight.

### Hashtags
- Minimal. Often none. When used, keep to 1-3 and make them meaningful
  (e.g., #EffectiveScrum for Scrum posts). Avoid hashtag salad.
- Evidence: the Q1 2026 report found posts with more than 3 hashtags performed 71% worse than posts with none. The algorithm already reads your keywords, so extra hashtags add little and can signal a weaker creator.

### Calls to Action
- Genuine engagement requests over performative ones ("Looking for anecdotes about..."
  beats "What do you think? Comment below!"). Generic "What do you think?" prompts are dead -
  use a genuine question or a provocative statement instead.

### Links
- Put links in the post body, not in the comments. "Link in the comments" is the dead pattern.
- Links do not tank reach. The Q1 2026 report found posts with 1-3 links got 43% higher reach, and
  posts with more than 3 links got 441% higher reach, because link-heavy posts read as genuinely
  useful resource collections. Links to agilepainrelief.com are fine when the destination is genuinely useful.
- A natural fit for Mark: one link to his own article plus a few to the sources he footnoted.
- Quality bar: every link should be something the reader actually wants, not filler.

---

## Topic Modes (calibrate tone to the topic)

Posts generally fall into one of these modes. The voice is consistent; the lean differs.

### Scrum / Agile Practice
- **Tone**: Educational, helpful, empathetic to struggles.
- **Evidence**: Experience-based, practitioner stories, anti-patterns observed in the wild.
- **Goal**: Help readers fix problems in their teams.
- **Structure**: Often a problem + misdiagnosis + what actually works.
- **Hashtags**: Regular (e.g., #EffectiveScrum).

### AI / GenAI / LLMs in Software and Scrum
- **Tone**: Skeptical pragmatist -- not anti-AI, not hype. Measured, analytical.
- **Evidence**: Research-and-data-based (e.g., the 19%/20% perception-gap study, DORA rollback
  signals). Cite specifics when possible.
- **Goal**: Question assumptions; surface hidden costs; ground hype in evidence.
- **Structure**: Provocative claim + counter-evidence + implication. "Hidden costs nobody talks
  about" framing works well. Always connect back to Scrum values (collaboration, human judgement,
  context over speed) when relevant.
- **Hashtags**: Minimal, sometimes none.
- **Watch for**: Drift into dismissive or mocking territory. Mark's position is "I'm not against
  GenAI, but let's be realistic." Acknowledge potential benefits before the "but".

### Personal / Travel / Seasonal
- **Tone**: Warm, conversational, light. Pub-with-coworkers voice at its purest.
- **Evidence**: Not required; this is connective tissue.
- **Goal**: Build relationship with the audience.
- **Watch for**: Too-long personal posts that lose their thread. Brevity is kindness.

### Workshop / Training / Business Announcements
- **Tone**: Direct, low-key. Inform, don't sell.
- **Watch for**: Salesy language, exclamation marks, "amazing opportunity" energy.

If a post spans modes (common for AI-meets-Scrum posts), apply both rubrics.

---

## Critique Output Format

Structure the response like this:

### Overall Impression
[2-3 sentences: Does this land? What's the main issue?]

### Voice & Tone
[Does this sound like Mark? Where does it, where doesn't it?]

### Hook & Opening
[Is the first line doing enough work? Specific feedback.]

### Structure & Length
[Length check, one-clear-point check, flow.]

### Anti-Pattern Detections
For each:
> **Found**: "[exact quote]"
> **Issue**: [which anti-pattern, or why this grates]
> **Suggested fix**: "[rewritten phrase in Mark's voice]"

### Terminology & Language
[Flag issues only: ScrumMaster spelling, GenAI/LLM usage, capitalisation, buzzwords, emdash. If the draft gets all of these right, omit this section - Mark knows his own rules and doesn't need praise for following them.]

### Engagement Mechanics
[Emoji count and use, hashtag choice, CTA quality.]

### Practitioner Takeaway
[Does the post hand the reader something they can do, think about, or test in their own work? Scrum and GenAI posts land harder with a closing line that gives the reader an action or a frame to apply. Not every post needs one - personal and seasonal posts rarely do - so flag only when one would clearly help, and don't force one where it doesn't fit.]

### Strengths
[Specific phrases or moves that nail the voice. Be concrete.]

### Priority Fixes
[Top 3-5 changes ranked by impact, with brief rationale. These should be the improvements
Mark would actually make before posting.]

---

## Reference Material

- `APR/Efforts/Newsletter/` -- any newsletter file demonstrates Mark's voice at length.
  Good calibration if a draft feels off and you want to recalibrate before critiquing.
- `Skills/APR/newsletter-reviewer/SKILL.md` -- the longer-form sibling of this skill. Voice profile
  and anti-pattern list overlap; this skill is the LinkedIn-shaped subset.
- `OutsideContent/Generated/State of the LinkedIn Algorithm Q1 2026 - Report and Call Notes.md` --
  the evidence behind the length, links, hashtag, and emoji guidance here (Q1 2026 algorithm data plus
  Mike Schmitz's commentary). Read it if you want the numbers or to re-check a convention.

---

## Important Notes

- Mark does all his own writing. This skill helps him sharpen drafts, not replace them.
- The goal is to help Mark sound more like himself. His quirks, self-deprecation, and
  practitioner-grounded examples are features, not bugs.
- When in doubt, lean toward "a knowledgeable friend at a pub" over "a consultant on a panel".
- Mark's LinkedIn audience is ScrumMasters, Agile Coaches, Product Owners, managers, and
  adjacent practitioners. They often know what to do but lack the influence to change it.
  Empathy for that tension matters.

## 1. Blog — GenAI code quality / bluffing
**URL:** /blog/genai-code-quality-fundamental-flaws-and-how-bluffing-makes-it-worse/

### Option A — the data, and why it's structural
AI-generated code has 1.7x more issues, and the GenAI code quality gap is turning into a chasm. That's not a random number, it's from a CodeRabbit research report, which also shows 30-41% more tech debt and 39% more cognitive complexity.

These problems are structural. Training focuses on pass/fail: does the code compile, does it pass the tests? There's no reward for writing code that's easy to maintain. Some teams think TDD is the fix, and others suggest we can code review our way out of this. We can't code review our way out of this mess, because that just puts the burden on humans to tidy up the mess that the AI created.

So instead of trying to build quality into code faster, why don't we work on making sure we know what the right product is first? When it comes to the code itself, give the models smaller, more focused tasks, and start with a small set of acceptance criteria for a single feature.

What are you doing to survive this mess? I genuinely want to know.

#AIinSoftwareDevelopment

### Option B — the bluffing
GenAI code quality problems start with how the models are trained. Training focuses on pass/fail: does the code compile, does it pass the tests? There's no reward for writing code that's easy to maintain. Worse, 0-1 grading schemes incentivize guessing over admitting a lack of knowledge, so the models learn to "bluff" with plausible but overconfident best guesses.

OX Security likens this to an army of junior developers, fast and functional, but lacking architectural judgment. So what about TDD? It helps, but it's solving the wrong problem. It forces you to understand the problem before accepting the solution, but it can't tell you whether the feature itself is waste.

The models won't fix themselves, and the labs aren't prioritizing what matters: well-designed architecture, maintainability, security in context, and respect for your codebase. Until that changes, we deal with what we've got, one small and focused task at a time.

#AIinSoftwareDevelopment #Agile

---

## 2. Blog — Sprint Backlog
**URL:** /blog/the-humble-sprint-backlog/

### Option A — ownership
Sadly, many Scrum Teams simply use whatever their online Scrum tool feeds them for their Sprint Backlog. This harms the Team's capacity for engagement, because it reinforces the sense that Scrum is happening to them, not something that they choose.

Since the Sprint Backlog is solely for the Scrum Team to organize their own work during a Sprint, they are the only ones who create, change, and manage it, not a tool, and not an outsider. Many teams also benefit by stealing a page from the Kanban playbook and limiting Work in Progress. Teams that limit WIP to two or three Product Backlog Items tend to collaborate more, cross-skill faster, and eventually eliminate the problem of having unfinished work at the end of Sprint.

Good Scrum teams know that they own the Sprint Backlog. Great teams experiment every few Sprints to find what they can do to make it even better.

#Scrum #ScrumMaster

### Option B — anti-patterns
A couple of Sprint Backlog anti-patterns are worth naming, because they're common and they're quiet.

When the Sprint Backlog is created during Sprint Planning, some teams decide who will work on which item. When all items are pre-assigned to team members, we have just planned for the first bottleneck.

The Sprint Backlog also loses its value when it's used for external purposes like reporting. When leadership uses it to look over the shoulders of the people doing the work, it often leads to overloading the Sprint Backlog with details that undermine and eliminate transparency. The Sprint Backlog is used only by the Scrum Team, and is not intended to be viewed by anyone else. It's a plan by and for the Developers, a real-time picture of the work they plan to accomplish to achieve the Sprint Goal.

#Scrum #ProductOwner

---

## 3. Glossary — AI and Skill Atrophy
**URL:** /glossary/ai-skill-atrophy/

### Option A — the knowledge cliff
We're losing skills because we don't use them, and we're not growing the developers of the future.

When you use an LLM to make a decision you could make without the LLM, you gain a sense of false confidence. The easier it is to prompt an LLM to produce an answer, the less we develop the skill, and this affects junior people more than senior people, since they have less overall experience to base their skills on.

NASA has been through this recently. They want to build big rockets again, and they have mountains of documentation, literally 2900 cubic feet, but they don't have the understanding and tacit knowledge to use it. This is a knowledge cliff, and the software industry is headed to one.

So before automating with AI, ask: do we understand the domain well enough to evaluate the output? The more we use AI, the more critical thinking becomes important.

#AIinSoftwareDevelopment #Leadership

### Option B — pilots and radiologists
In the academic literature, losing the skills you stop practising is called Deskilling, and we've watched it happen outside software before.

In radiology, AI assistants help detect abnormalities in medical images. In theory, they detect problems faster and don't get tired. But too much reliance on AI leaves the radiologist unable to detect on their own. Bad enough for the senior radiologists, but even worse for new doctors who never built the underlying understanding.

Pilots have been through this too. With the advent of autopilot, instrument landing systems, and automated flight management systems, they reduced the need for certain piloting skills. To combat this, they increased the amount of training and simulator time for pilots to maintain their certifications.

Software is walking toward the same cliff, except we're cutting practice instead of protecting it. The more we use AI, the more critical thinking becomes important.

#AIinSoftwareDevelopment

---

## 4. Glossary — Definition of Done
**URL:** /glossary/definition-of-done/

### Option A — the pressure
The 2020 Scrum Guide elevated Definition of Done to a formal commitment for the Increment. In other words, Done is not optional: it is the team's promise about what "complete" means.

The hardest problem to achieving Done is pressure to deliver more features. As the pressure builds, the team may respond by compromising on Done. In the short term this appears to be fine, as they appear to get more work finished. In the long run, the increase in bugs inevitably offsets the value of the added work, and each shortcut accumulates as technical debt, making future work slower and more error-prone.

That's why the team need to start Sprint Planning with a clear understanding of their own Definition of Done, and only take on work that they can bring to truly Done.

#Scrum #ScrumMaster

### Option B — undone work
When a product is not truly releasable at the end of Sprint, the difference is often referred to as Undone work. Why is this a problem? It's a problem because it reduces transparency. The Product Owner and clients think the team have completed work on those User Stories, yet the work isn't complete.

Here's how that plays out later: a bug is found several Sprints after the code is written, and now new code relies on the defective behaviour. Or, missing a security audit, the application is susceptible to a SQL injection attack. When a team has a rigorous Definition of Done, the Product Owner should be able to release a new version of the product at the end of every Sprint.

One caution: Definition of Done is for the Scrum Team to understand the quality of the product they're creating. It's not a reporting standard, and using it as one leads to micro management.

#Scrum #ProductOwner

## 5. Newsletter — "Are You Planning Enough?" (2026-04-02)
**URL:** /newsletter-subscribe/
*(Newsletters aren't published as individual pages, so this drives to signup. Swap in a web-archive link if you'd rather point at the issue itself.)*

### Option A — 5% vs 20%
By default, as humans we spend about 5% of our time planning and 95% implementing those plans. The research suggests that the number should be closer to 20% planning and 80% action.

I found that in Chris Bailey's book Intentional, which I read on a hiking trip in the Canary Islands that turned into a reading trip when a storm rolled in. Thinking about Scrum, all of Sprint Planning, Review, Retrospective, and Daily Scrum are about planning and goal attainment. Officially, they're supposed to occupy 10% of the Sprint, and Backlog Refinement takes up another 3-5%. Scrum anticipated the research that Chris found for his book by more than a decade.

When we see teams first adopt Scrum, there is often pushback: too much time spent on planning and not enough time doing. I've always known the pushback was misplaced, and now I have research to support it.

#Scrum #Agile

### Option B — planning in a GenAI world
Many teams are using GenAI to rip through their Product Backlog without considering whether the work has any value. Shipping unproven features faster is not winning.

By default, as humans we spend about 5% of our time planning and 95% implementing those plans, when the research suggests it should be closer to 20% planning and 80% action. Scrum already builds that in: Sprint Planning, Review, Retrospective, and Daily Scrum are all about planning and goal attainment, and Backlog Refinement adds a little more.

As we move into a world where GenAI can help us do some of the heavy lifting, intentions and planning will be ever more important. To thrive in this new world, we will need better Product Ownership and quality, not just more output.

#AIinSoftwareDevelopment #ProductOwner

## 1. Blog — GenAI code quality / bluffing (glass 1/3 full)
**URL:** /blog/genai-code-quality-fundamental-flaws-and-how-bluffing-makes-it-worse/

### Option A — the data
AI-generated code has 1.7x more issues, and the quality gap is turning into a chasm.

That's not a random number. It's from a CodeRabbit research report: 30-41% more tech debt, 39% more cognitive complexity. And the flaws are structural. Training rewards code that compiles and passes tests. There's no reward for code that's easy to maintain, so the model optimises for "does it work" and nothing else.

You can't code review your way out of that. That just puts the burden on humans to tidy up the mess the model made.

I use these tools daily. The fix isn't more speed: give the model smaller, more focused tasks, and make sure you know what the right product is first.

#AIinSoftwareDevelopment

### Option B — the bluffing
GenAI doesn't write bad code because it's dumb. It writes bad code because of how it's rewarded.

Training and evaluation reward code that compiles and passes the tests. 0-1 grading schemes reward guessing over admitting a lack of knowledge, so the model learns to bluff: plausible, overconfident best guesses. OX Security calls it an army of junior developers, fast and functional, but lacking architectural judgment.

TDD helps. Code review helps. Neither fixes a structural problem baked in at training time.

Genuinely useful for the dull work, oversold on the rest. Knowing where GenAI erodes quality is how you use it well.

#AIinSoftwareDevelopment #Agile

---

## 2. Blog — Sprint Backlog
**URL:** /blog/the-humble-sprint-backlog/

### Option A — ownership
If your Sprint Backlog is whatever your online tool feeds you, it isn't really yours.

The Sprint Backlog is created by the Team, for the Team. When you just accept what the tool spits out, it reinforces the sense that Scrum is happening to them, not something they choose. That quietly kills engagement.

Good Scrum teams know they own the Sprint Backlog. Great teams experiment every few Sprints to make it better: steal a WIP limit from Kanban, add an interruptions lane, pin the Sprint Goal at the top.

Own it first. Then improve it.

#Scrum #ScrumMaster

### Option B — anti-pattern
The fastest way to hobble a Sprint Backlog: pre-assign every item on day one.

When all items are pre-assigned to team members, you've just planned for the first bottleneck. Same story when it becomes a reporting tool and leadership starts looking over shoulders. It loses its value.

The Sprint Backlog is a plan by and for the Developers. It's used only by the Scrum Team, not as a status report for anyone else.

Keep it the team's. Limit WIP. Let people pull the work they're ready for.

#Scrum #ProductOwner

**URL:** /glossary/ai-skill-atrophy/

NASA wants to build big rockets again. They have 2,900 cubic feet of documentation and not enough people who still understand it.

Before you automate with GenAI, ask: do we understand this well enough to judge the output? The more we use AI, the more critical thinking matters.

#AIinSoftwareDevelopment #Leadership

### Option B — the pilots
We're losing skills because we don't use them.

The easier it is to prompt an LLM for an answer, the less we build the skill ourselves. Academics call it deskilling. Pilots hit this decades ago with autopilot, and their fix was more training and simulator time, not less. Software is walking into the same trap, except we're cutting practice instead of protecting it.

GenAI is genuinely useful for the dull work. Just don't let it quietly take the practice your juniors need to become seniors.

#AIinSoftwareDevelopment

---

## 4. Glossary — Definition of Done
**URL:** /glossary/definition-of-done/

### Option A — the pressure
The moment the pressure builds, most teams quietly negotiate their Definition of Done downward.

In the short term it looks fine: more stories finished. In the long run the bugs offset the value, and each shortcut accumulates as technical debt that makes future work slower and more error-prone.

Done is not optional. It's the team's promise about what "complete" actually means. Work that looks finished but doesn't meet Done hasn't saved you time, it's just hidden the cost.

Only take on work in Sprint Planning that you can bring to truly Done.

#Scrum #ScrumMaster

### Option B — undone work
"Done" and "looks done" are not the same thing, and the gap has a name: Undone work.

The Product Owner thinks the story shipped. It didn't. A bug surfaces three Sprints later and new code already relies on the broken behaviour. Skip the security review and hello, SQL injection. Undone work reduces transparency, and that's the real damage.

A rigorous Definition of Done is what lets the Product Owner release at the end of every Sprint with confidence. And it's for the team, not a reporting standard. Use it to report upward and you just breed micromanagement.

#Scrum #ProductOwner

---

## 5. Newsletter — "Are You Planning Enough?" (2026-04-02)
**URL:** /newsletter-subscribe/
*(Newsletters aren't published as individual pages, so this drives to signup. Swap in a web-archive link if you'd rather point at the issue itself.)*

### Option A — the 5% vs 20%
By default, we humans spend about 5% of our time planning and 95% doing. The research says it should be closer to 20% planning, 80% action.

I found that in Chris Bailey's book Intentional, on a hiking trip that turned into a reading trip when a storm rolled in. Then it clicked: Scrum anticipated this by more than a decade. Sprint Planning, Review, Retrospective, Daily Scrum, plus Backlog Refinement land around 13-15% of a Sprint spent on planning and goal attainment.

The usual pushback when teams adopt Scrum is "too much planning, not enough doing." Turns out that pushback is misplaced, and now there's research to back it up.

#Scrum #Agile

### Option B — planning in a GenAI world

Shipping unproven features faster is not winning. We default to about 5% planning and 95% doing, when the research points closer to 20% planning as where goals actually get met. Scrum already builds that in: Planning, Review, Retro, Daily Scrum, Refinement.

To thrive in a world where GenAI does more of the heavy lifting, we'll need better Product Ownership and quality, not just more output. Spend the 20%. Decide what's worth building before you let the machine build it.

#AIinSoftwareDevelopment #ProductOwner

### Option A — the pressure
The 2020 Scrum Guide elevated Definition of Done to a formal commitment for the Increment. In other words, Done is not optional: it is the team's promise about what "complete" means.

The hardest problem to achieving Done is pressure to deliver more features. As the pressure builds, the team may respond by compromising on Done. In the short term this appears to be fine, as they appear to get more work finished. In the long run, the increase in bugs inevitably offsets the value of the added work, and each shortcut accumulates as technical debt, making future work slower and more error-prone.

That's why the team need to start Sprint Planning with a clear understanding of their own Definition of Done, and only take on work that they can bring to truly Done.

#Scrum #ScrumMaster

### Option B — undone work
When a product is not truly releasable at the end of Sprint, the difference is often referred to as Undone work. Why is this a problem? It's a problem because it reduces transparency. The Product Owner and clients think the team have completed work on those User Stories, yet the work isn't complete.

Here's how that plays out later: a bug is found several Sprints after the code is written, and now new code relies on the defective behaviour. Or, missing a security audit, the application is susceptible to a SQL injection attack. When a team has a rigorous Definition of Done, the Product Owner should be able to release a new version of the product at the end of every Sprint.

One caution: Definition of Done is for the Scrum Team to understand the quality of the product they're creating. It's not a reporting standard, and using it as one leads to micro management.

#Scrum #ProductOwner

---

## 5. Newsletter — "Are You Planning Enough?" (2026-04-02)
**URL:** /newsletter-subscribe/
*(Newsletters aren't published as individual pages, so this drives to signup. Swap in a web-archive link if you'd rather point at the issue itself.)*

### Option A — 5% vs 20%
By default, as humans we spend about 5% of our time planning and 95% implementing those plans. The research suggests that the number should be closer to 20% planning and 80% action.

I found that in Chris Bailey's book Intentional, which I read on a hiking trip in the Canary Islands that turned into a reading trip when a storm rolled in. Thinking about Scrum, all of Sprint Planning, Review, Retrospective, and Daily Scrum are about planning and goal attainment. Officially, they're supposed to occupy 10% of the Sprint, and Backlog Refinement takes up another 3-5%. Scrum anticipated the research that Chris found for his book by more than a decade.

When we see teams first adopt Scrum, there is often pushback: too much time spent on planning and not enough time doing. I've always known the pushback was misplaced, and now I have research to support it.

#Scrum #Agile

### Option B — planning in a GenAI world
Many teams are using GenAI to rip through their Product Backlog without considering whether the work has any value. Shipping unproven features faster is not winning.

By default, as humans we spend about 5% of our time planning and 95% implementing those plans, when the research suggests it should be closer to 20% planning and 80% action. Scrum already builds that in: Sprint Planning, Review, Retrospective, and Daily Scrum are all about planning and goal attainment, and Backlog Refinement adds a little more.

As we move into a world where GenAI can help us do some of the heavy lifting, intentions and planning will be ever more important. To thrive in this new world, we will need better Product Ownership and quality, not just more output.

#AIinSoftwareDevelopment #ProductOwner

They read them. They nod. They say "yes, I understand."

And every person is picturing something different.

That's the trap with using GenAI to write your user stories, epics, or acceptance criteria. These artifacts were never the point. They exist to help people to reach a shared understanding through conversation. When the story arrives looking finished, the conversation never happens, and you get false agreement that falls apart as soon as the work starts.

This predates GenAI. Product Owners could always bash out a polished product backlog item and mistake nodding for understanding. GenAI just manufactures that false consensus faster.

Where can GenAI help in Refinement: ask it to pressure-test a story. Does it meet INVEST? Is the "why" clear? Where's the ambiguity? Stuck splitting something big? Have it suggest splits. Most of them will be wrong, but it can be a good spark. Let it question your prioritization.

The difference: those uses spark the conversation. Generating the stories replaces it.

I use these tools daily. Knowing where they erode shared understanding is how you use them well.

How GenAI fits across all five Scrum events and activities:

name: social-posting-conventions
description: Shared reference (not a triggered skill). Canonical conventions for the evergreen-posting and social-media-adapt skills — character limits, threading, hashtags, URLs, and style. Read this first; it is the single source of truth. Both skills defer to it.
---

# Social Posting Conventions (shared reference)

Single source of truth for the two social-posting skills:

- **`evergreen-posting`** — batch JSON array, one set across LinkedIn / Mastodon / Bluesky.
- **`social-media-adapt`** — a single LinkedIn post adapted into Mastodon / Bluesky threaded JSON.

The **`social-media-posting` repo (the Buffer pipeline) is the enforcement authority.** It validates and rejects posts. If a skill or this doc disagrees with what the pipeline actually does, the pipeline wins and this doc gets corrected, not the other way round.

## Character limits (hard)

| Platform | Limit per post/part | URLs |
|---|---|---|
| LinkedIn | 2000 | counted at full length |
| Mastodon | 500 | counted as a fixed 23 |
| Bluesky  | **290** | counted at full length |

Bluesky's platform hard limit is 300, but the pipeline caps at **290** — posts at 296-300 chars empirically get rejected by Buffer, so we keep a 10-char safety margin. Always validate Bluesky against 290, not 300.

The pipeline appends the `url` field to each platform's body, and the link counts toward the limit. **Bluesky and LinkedIn count it at full length** (Buffer no longer shortens by default since 2025-04, and Bluesky's API counts the raw URL); **Mastodon counts every URL as a fixed 23.** So on Bluesky the canonical URL plus its UTM (~100-130 chars) comes out of the 290 budget: keep Bluesky bodies short (~150). Never pre-shorten a URL yourself.

## Threading

| Platform | Parts |
|---|---|
| Mastodon | 1-2 preferred, 3 max, never 4 |
| Bluesky  | 2-3 max |

`evergreen-posting` uses a single string per platform (no threading). `social-media-adapt` uses a `parts` array.

## Hashtags

**Always, on every post:**

- `#AIinSoftwareDevelopment`

**Add when the topic matches (canonical topic list):**

`#Agile` `#Scrum` `#ScrumMaster` `#ProductOwner` `#TechnicalDebt` `#TeamWork` `#Leadership`

**Per-platform counts:** LinkedIn 2-4 · Mastodon 2-3 · Bluesky 2. Hashtags go at the end of the final post/part.

## Emoji

Use emoji on every platform (LinkedIn, Mastodon, Bluesky), lightly.

- **1-2 per post.** An opening emoji to catch the eye; an optional second to mark a structural turn (e.g. the constructive pivot after a critique). More than two reads as cluttered.
- **Never on a vulnerability beat or a serious moment** (a confession, a burnout point) - it undercuts the weight.
- **Bluesky:** emoji count against the 290-char budget, so only spend them when they earn the space.
- Why: they add colour to otherwise-uniform body text and pull the eye to a key point or the CTA. That is the mechanism; it does not license overuse.

## URLs and links

- **The link goes in the post body on every platform, LinkedIn included.** There is no "link in the first comment" — that pattern is retired.
- **`evergreen-posting` format:** never inline a URL in the body. Put it in the `url` field; the pipeline places it in each platform's body. **`social-media-adapt` format:** the URL goes inline in the body (Mastodon and Bluesky always carry the link inline).
- **Never shorten URLs.** Buffer shortens them automatically.
- **Never pre-fill UTM params.** The pipeline appends per-platform UTM (`?utm_source=...&utm_campaign=archive-reshare`) to `agilepainrelief.com` URLs; pre-filling locks the URL to one platform.
- **Cover images:** in the batch format leave `image: ""`; the pipeline scrapes `og:image` from the linked page.

## Style

- **No em dashes.** Use a colon, comma, semicolon, or restructure. (Project-wide rule.)
- **No non-breaking spaces (U+00A0).** ASCII spaces only.
- Straight quotes and apostrophes are fine in JSON values.
- **Never invent stats.** Every number must trace to a real source (a quiz-hook seed or the linked post).

-    "linkedin": "💬 You hand the team a clean list of GenAI-generated user stories.

They read them. They nod. They say "yes, I understand."

And every person is picturing something different.

That's the trap with using GenAI to write your user stories, epics, or acceptance criteria. These artifacts were never the point. They exist to help people to reach a shared understanding through conversation. When the story arrives looking finished, the conversation never happens, and you get false agreement that falls apart as soon as the work starts.

This predates GenAI. Product Owners could always bash out a polished product backlog item and mistake nodding for understanding. GenAI just manufactures that false consensus faster.

Where can GenAI help in Refinement: ask it to pressure-test a story. Does it meet INVEST? Is the "why" clear? Where's the ambiguity? Stuck splitting something big? Have it suggest splits. Most of them will be wrong, but it can be a good spark. Let it question your prioritization.

The difference: those uses spark the conversation. Generating the stories replaces it.

I use these tools daily. Knowing where they erode shared understanding is how you use them well.

How GenAI fits across all five Scrum events and activities:

+    "linkedin": "🃏 GenAI code quality problems start with how the models are trained. Training focuses on pass/fail: does the code compile, does it pass the tests? There's no reward for writing code that's easy to maintain. Worse, 0-1 grading schemes incentivize guessing over admitting a lack of knowledge, so the models learn to "bluff" with plausible but overconfident best guesses.

OX Security likens this to an army of junior developers, fast and functional, but lacking architectural judgment. So what about TDD? It helps, but it's solving the wrong problem. It forces you to understand the problem before accepting the solution, but it can't tell you whether the feature itself is waste.

The next release from Anthropic or OpenAI won't magically solve the problem. The labs aren't prioritizing well-designed architecture, maintainability, security in context, and respect for your codebase. Until that changes, we deal with what we've got, one small and focused task at a time.

+    "linkedin": "📋 Sprint Backlog's are Scrum's most misunderstood artifact. They're not a list of tickets or tasks. (thanks JIRA.) They're intended to be a tool for the team to understand what is going on in their work and how it is progressing. A couple of Sprint Backlog anti-patterns are worth naming, because they're common and they're quiet.

When the Sprint Backlog is created during Sprint Planning, some teams decide who will work on which item. When all items are pre-assigned to team members, we have just planned for the first bottleneck.

The Sprint Backlog also loses its value when it's used for external purposes like reporting. When leadership uses it to look over the shoulders of the people doing the work, it often leads to overloading the Sprint Backlog with details that undermine and eliminate transparency. The Sprint Backlog is used only by the Scrum Team, and is not intended to be viewed by anyone else. It's a plan by and for the Developers, a real-time picture of the work they plan to accomplish to achieve the Sprint Goal.

Which Sprint Backlog anti-pattern have you seen the most?

+    "linkedin": "📉 In the academic literature, losing the skills you stop practising is called Deskilling, and we've watched it happen outside software before.

In radiology, AI assistants help detect abnormalities in medical images. In theory, they detect problems faster and don't get tired. But too much reliance on AI leaves the radiologist unable to detect on their own. Bad enough for the senior radiologists, but even worse for new doctors who never built the underlying understanding.

Pilots have been through this too. With the advent of autopilot, instrument landing systems, and automated flight management systems, they reduced the need for certain piloting skills. To combat this, they increased the amount of training and simulator time for pilots to maintain their certifications.

Software is walking toward the same cliff, except we're cutting practice instead of protecting it. The more we use AI, the more critical thinking becomes important.

29	
30	### Option B — the bluffing
31	GenAI code quality problems start with how the models are trained. Training focuses on pass/fail: does the code compile, does it pass the tests? There's no reward for writing code that's easy to maintain. Worse, 0-1 grading schemes incentivize guessing over admitting a lack of knowledge, so the models learn to "bluff" with plausible but overconfident best guesses.
32	
33	OX Security likens this to an army of junior developers, fast and functional, but lacking architectural judgment. So what about TDD? It helps, but it's solving the wrong problem. It forces you to understand the problem before accepting the solution, but it can't tell you whether the feature itself is waste.
34	
35	The next release from Anthropic/OpenAI won't magically solve the problem. The labs aren't prioritizing: well-designed architecture, maintainability, security in context, and respect for your codebase. Until that changes, we deal with what we've got, one small and focused task at a time.
36	
37	What are you doing to survive this mess? I genuinely want to know.
38	
39	#AIinSoftwareDevelopment #Agile
40	
41	---
42	
43	## 2. Blog — Sprint Backlog
44	**URL:** /blog/the-humble-sprint-backlog/
45	
46	### Option A — ownership
47	Sadly, many Scrum Teams simply use whatever their online Scrum tool feeds them for their Sprint Backlog. This harms the Team's capacity for engagement, because it reinforces the sense that Scrum is happening to them, not something that they choose.
48	
49	Since the Sprint Backlog is solely for the Scrum Team to organize their own work during a Sprint, they are the only ones who create, change, and manage it, not a tool, and not an outsider. Many teams also benefit by stealing a page from the Kanban playbook and limiting Work in Progress. Teams that limit WIP to two or three Product Backlog Items tend to collaborate more, cross-skill faster, and eventually eliminate the problem of having unfinished work at the end of Sprint.
50	
51	Good Scrum teams know that they own the Sprint Backlog. Great teams experiment every few Sprints to find what they can do to make it even better.
52	
53	#Scrum #ScrumMaster
54	
55	### Option B — anti-patterns
56	Sprint Backlog's are Scrum's most misunderstood artifact. They're not a list of tickets or tasks. (thanks JIRA.) They're intended to be a tool for the team to understand what is going on in their work and how it is progressing. A couple of Sprint Backlog anti-patterns are worth naming, because they're common and they're quiet.
57	
58	When the Sprint Backlog is created during Sprint Planning, some teams decide who will work on which item. When all items are pre-assigned to team members, we have just planned for the first bottleneck.
59	
60	The Sprint Backlog also loses its value when it's used for external purposes like reporting. When leadership uses it to look over the shoulders of the people doing the work, it often leads to overloading the Sprint Backlog with details that undermine and eliminate transparency. The Sprint Backlog is used only by the Scrum Team, and is not intended to be viewed by anyone else. It's a plan by and for the Developers, a real-time picture of the work they plan to accomplish to achieve the Sprint Goal.
61	
62	Which Sprint Backlog anti-pattern have you seen the most?
63	
64	#Scrum #ProductOwner
65	
66	---
67	
68	## 3. Glossary — AI and Skill Atrophy
69	**URL:** /glossary/ai-skill-atrophy/
70	
71	### Option A — the knowledge cliff
72	We're losing skills because we don't use them, and we're not growing the developers of the future.
73	
74	When you use an LLM to make a decision you could make without the LLM, you gain a sense of false confidence. The easier it is to prompt an LLM to produce an answer, the less we develop the skill, and this affects junior people more than senior people, since they have less overall experience to base their skills on.
75	
76	NASA has been through this recently. They want to build big rockets again, and they have mountains of documentation, literally 2900 cubic feet, but they don't have the understanding and tacit knowledge to use it. This is a knowledge cliff, and the software industry is headed to one.
77	
78	So before automating with AI, ask: do we understand the domain well enough to evaluate the output? The more we use AI, the more critical thinking becomes important.
79	
80	#AIinSoftwareDevelopment #Leadership
81	
82	### Option B — pilots and radiologists
83	In the academic literature, losing the skills you stop practising is called Deskilling, and we've watched it happen outside software before.
84	
85	In radiology, AI assistants help detect abnormalities in medical images. In theory, they detect problems faster and don't get tired. But too much reliance on AI leaves the radiologist unable to detect on their own. Bad enough for the senior radiologists, but even worse for new doctors who never built the underlying understanding.
86	
87	Pilots have been through this too. With the advent of autopilot, instrument landing systems, and automated flight management systems, they reduced the need for certain piloting skills. To combat this, they increased the amount of training and simulator time for pilots to maintain their certifications.
88	
89	Software is walking toward the same cliff, except we're cutting practice instead of protecting it. The more we use AI, the more critical thinking becomes important.
90	
91	#AIinSoftwareDevelopment
92	
93	---
94	
95	## 4. Glossary — Definition of Done
96	**URL:** /glossary/definition-of-done/
97	
98	### Option A — the pressure
99	The 2020 Scrum Guide elevated Definition of Done to a formal commitment for the Increment. In other words, Done is not optional: it is the team's promise about what "complete" means.
100

1	---
2	title: "Canada's AI Strategy Mistakes Adoption for Productivity"
3	date: "2026-07-10"
4	categories:
5	  - "artificial-intelligence"
6	coverImage: '@/content/blog/canadas-ai-strategy-mistakes-adoption-for-productivity/images/GenAIGamblingWithYourProductivity.png'
7	excerpt: There is a massive gap between claiming AI will boost productivity and actually fixing bottlenecks. Lessons from Canada's healthcare system and Humber River Hospital.
8	---
9	import Figure from '@/components/global/figure.astro';
10	import Loopy from '@/components/global/Loopy.astro';
11	import genAIGambling from '@/content/blog/canadas-ai-strategy-mistakes-adoption-for-productivity/images/GenAIGamblingWithYourProductivity.png';
12	
13	Canada has a real productivity problem. We have for decades. In 1984, the Canadian economy was 88% as productive as the US per hour worked. In 2022, it had fallen to 71%.[^1]
14	
15	The new AI strategy is an attempt to fix that. It promises a 3 percent increase in GDP, from labour productivity. “Increase Canada’s business adoption of AI from 12 percent today to 60 percent by 2034, through boosting SMEs and business adoption supports.”[^2] I’m reminded of the mineshaft gap in Dr Strangelove (Stanley Kubrick was satirizing the military focus on the missile gap in the 1950s). Adoption of AI doesn’t make an organization more productive. I made [the same argument about the federal government](/blog/will-ai-make-the-federal-government-more-efficient-or-just-more-busy/): dropping AI onto a broken process just automates the mess. A target like this invites AI washing: measure success by adoption rate and organizations will claim they're "doing AI" to hit the number, whether or not anything meaningful changes.
16	
17	Saying a new technology will magically make us more productive doesn’t make it so.
18	
19	## Sectors
20	The strategy names sectors where AI will create “outsized value”: healthcare, energy and natural resources, transportation, agriculture, and manufacturing. Why these sectors? Based on what evidence?
21	
22	<Figure
23	  src={genAIGambling}
24	  alt="Illustration of a robot labelled AI next to a pair of dice, headed “Canada's AI Strategy: Will AI Make Us More Productive?” and captioned “Gambling with Your Productivity”"
25	  caption="Naming sectors without evidence of where AI actually helps is a bet, not a plan."
26	/>
27	
28	There are many ways AI could help and harm in all of these sectors. The strategy doesn’t say anything useful about how AI will help.
29	
30	## Healthcare
31	I will focus on the health sector, because it’s the one we hear about most often. In Ontario, the stories are of emergency rooms overflowing. In some rural communities, the emergency rooms operate on reduced hours due to staffing shortages. To make the emergency room more efficient, we might try to use AI to help in the triage process. Assuming the AI doesn’t make any mistakes (unwise assumption), we’ve sped up the triage process. Unfortunately if the hospital is operating at 100% or more of capacity in terms of the number of beds, speeding triage doesn’t help. It helps a handful leave faster but doesn’t make a meaningful difference.
32	
33	Our mistake? We tackled the emergency room problem in isolation.
34	
35	Putting on our [Systems Thinking](/blog/genai-systems-thinking-team-problems/) hat, we want to ask two questions:
36	- Why are there so many people visiting emergency rooms?
37	- Why are hospital beds so full?
38	
39	### Hospital beds
40	- Low population to hospital bed ratio
41	- Waiting lists for long term care
42	- Staffing shortages
43	
44	### Emergency Room Volume
45	- Lack of family doctor
46	- Lack of family doctor turns simple problems into more complex problems, which in turn might result in a hospital stay
47	- Unsure where to go: walk in clinic? Emergency?
48	- Seasonal flu et al
49	
50	These factors don’t sit in neat boxes; they feed each other. Drag any node in the diagram below to see how a change ripples through the system. Notice the reinforcing loop on the left: admin burden burns doctors out, so fewer family doctors remain, which piles more admin on those still practising. That shortage pushes people into the ER, and the beds, our real bottleneck, stay full whether or not triage runs faster.
51	
52	<Loopy
53	  data="[[[1,440,270,0.5,%22Family%2520Doctors%22,3],[2,200,410,0.5,%22Admin%2520Burden%22,1],[3,200,150,0.5,%22Doctor%2520Burnout%22,0],[4,660,150,0.5,%22ER%2520Visits%22,2],[5,880,300,0.5,%22Bed%2520Occupancy%22,0],[6,660,430,0.5,%22LTC%2520Waitlist%22,5]],[[2,3,40,1],[3,1,40,-1],[1,2,150,-1],[1,4,-40,-1],[4,5,-40,1],[6,5,40,1]],[[200,500,%22Reinforcing%2520loop%22],[880,190,%22The%2520bottleneck%22]],7%5D"
54	  title="Causal loop diagram: why faster ER triage doesn't empty full hospital beds"
55	/>
56	
57	None of these problems will magically get fixed by AI. If we want our healthcare system to help us get well/stay well, look at the overall system.
58	
59	One example of a hospital taking a systemic approach? Humber River Hospital has a command centre where they’re paying attention[^3] to:
60	- Emergency Department volume
61	- Bed allocations and assignments
62	- Room cleaning
63	- Critical care capacity
64	- Surgical scheduling
65	- Discharge planning
66	
67	Reading the promotional PDF from GE[^4] the command centre is focused on getting the patients who need admission a bed faster and reducing pain, complications and secondary infections.
68	
69	GE promotes this system as using AI. However, the AI isn’t the central feature. The value of this system is that people in the hospital are paying constant attention to how the hospital is working. If there is a constraint, they make changes to reduce the problem. The command centre is staffed by a cross disciplinary group of people, so that there is enough knowledge in the room to make good decisions.
70	
71	AI is useful here, because they’ve studied the flow of the system. They’ve established useful metrics: getting people healthy and allowing them to leave hospital. Here’s the irony: the pattern-finding that actually helps predates ChatGPT and GenAI entirely. GE brands it “AI” but it’s not the AI the strategy is betting on.
72	
73	The material available in public is promotional so the actual effectiveness of the real system is something I can’t see.
74	
75	AI didn’t make Humber River Hospital more effective. Improving the flow in the system made it more effective. Predictive analytics is just a tool in this picture.
76	
77	### Family Doctors and GenAI
78	Earlier we noted that the lack of family doctors is a contributing factor to over capacity.
79	
80	After a full day of seeing patients, family doctors still have to write up charts documenting their findings, treatment and prescriptions. This is unpaid labour, the doctor is paid for the patient visit and the documentation is treated as overhead.
81	
82	Family doctors are already dealing with burnout, it turns out that OHIP payments in many cases don’t cover the realistic costs of running a clinic (rental, front office staff, medical equipment, computers, etc.) In an attempt to reduce the unpaid labour, many doctors I know have turned to GenAI transcription tools. There are clearly documented problems with some of these tools making mistakes with both the diagnoses and medications[^5]. Yet the physicians I know report saving a considerable amount of time. Possibly another example of [GenAI making us feel more productive](/blog/using-genai-to-code-not-so-fast/) without making a big difference.
83	
84	GenAI might help here, however we’ve solved a symptom. Family doctors are expected to run businesses (not their training) and are expected to handle a large number of administrative tasks along with seeing patients.
85	
86	Transcription tools may help, but they don’t solve the underlying problem. The administrative burden on family doctors is a major factor in their burnout.
87	
88	We need to fix the system, and not just the symptoms.
89	
90	## Not a Magic Wand
91	GenAI isn’t a magic wand and it isn’t a panacea. In the right context, it can be very useful. Used in the wrong place, it can [make an organization more fragile, not more resilient](/blog/is-ai-making-your-organization-fragile-or-more-resilient/).
92	
93	Humber River Hospital’s command centre is a good step in the right direction. If we want to make a meaningful difference in the healthcare system, we need to look wider than just an emergency room. In short, we want to understand why family doctors are leaving the profession. If we can’t keep them happy to stay in the profession, then we can’t expect to keep patients out of the emergency room. At the other end of the spectrum, since many hospital beds are occupied by patients waiting for long term care, we need to find compassionate ways to improve the long term care system. We may also need more hospital staff and more beds.
94	
95	The Healthcare system in Canada is just one example of many. We have a productivity problem, but we can’t just tell people to use GenAI and expect an improvement. If we want to improve productivity, we need to look at each organization as a system, understand the bottlenecks in the system and focus on eliminating that bottleneck.
96	
97	[^1]: Bank of Canada, [Time to Break the Glass: Fixing Canada's Productivity Problem](https://www.bankofcanada.ca/2024/03/time-to-break-the-glass-fixing-canadas-productivity-problem/)
98	[^2]: Innovation, Science and Economic Development Canada, [Canada's National Artificial Intelligence Strategy](https://ised-isde.canada.ca/site/ised/en/canadas-national-artificial-intelligence-strategy-ai-all)
99	[^3]: Humber River Hospital Foundation, [Humber River Hospital's Command Centre Has Created 23 Virtual Beds](https://www.hrhfoundation.ca/blog/humber-river-hospitals-command-centre-has-created-23-virtual-beds/)
100	[^4]: GE Healthcare, [Humber River Hospital Command Centre: One Year in Review](https://www.gehealthcare.com/content/dam/gehc/sitecore-migrated-assets/gehc/us/files/services/value-partnerships/20190121-humber-river-hospital-command-centre-one-year-in-review.pdf) (PDF)
101	[^5]: CBC News, [Medical AI transcriber for Ontario doctors 'hallucinated,' generated errors: auditor general](https://www.cbc.ca/news/canada/toronto/ai-scribe-system-hallucinations-9.7197049)
102	
103	*Image attribution: Agile Pain Relief Consulting (July 2026)*

---

Canada has a real productivity problem. We have for decades. In 1984, the Canadian economy was 88% as productive as the US per hour worked. In 2022, it had fallen to 71%.[^1]

The new AI strategy is an attempt to fix that. It promises a 3 percent increase in GDP, from labour productivity. “Increase Canada’s business adoption of AI from 12 percent today to 60 percent by 2034, through boosting SMEs and business adoption supports.”[^2] I’m reminded of the mineshaft gap in Dr Strangelove (Stanley Kubrick was satirizing the military focus on the missile gap in the 1950s). Adoption of AI doesn’t make an organization more productive. I made [the same argument about the federal government](/blog/will-ai-make-the-federal-government-more-efficient-or-just-more-busy/): dropping AI onto a broken process just automates the mess. A target like this invites AI washing: measure success by adoption rate and organizations will claim they're "doing AI" to hit the number, whether or not anything meaningful changes.

Saying a new technology will magically make us more productive doesn’t make it so.

## Sectors
The strategy names sectors where AI will create “outsized value”: healthcare, energy and natural resources, transportation, agriculture, and manufacturing. Why these sectors? Based on what evidence?

<Figure
  src={genAIGambling}
  alt="Illustration of a robot labelled AI next to a pair of dice, headed “Canada's AI Strategy: Will AI Make Us More Productive?” and captioned “Gambling with Your Productivity”"
  caption="Naming sectors without evidence of where AI actually helps is a bet, not a plan."
/>

There are many ways AI could help and harm in all of these sectors. The strategy doesn’t say anything useful about how AI will help.

## Healthcare
I will focus on the health sector, because it’s the one we hear about most often. In Ontario, the stories are of emergency rooms overflowing. In some rural communities, the emergency rooms operate on reduced hours due to staffing shortages. To make the emergency room more efficient, we might try to use AI to help in the triage process. Assuming the AI doesn’t make any mistakes (unwise assumption), we’ve sped up the triage process. Unfortunately if the hospital is operating at 100% or more of capacity in terms of the number of beds, speeding triage doesn’t help. It helps a handful leave faster but doesn’t make a meaningful difference.

Our mistake? We tackled the emergency room problem in isolation.

Putting on our [Systems Thinking](/blog/genai-systems-thinking-team-problems/) hat, we want to ask two questions:
- Why are there so many people visiting emergency rooms?
- Why are hospital beds so full?

### Hospital beds
- Low population to hospital bed ratio
- Waiting lists for long term care
- Staffing shortages

### Emergency Room Volume
- Lack of family doctor
- Lack of family doctor turns simple problems into more complex problems, which in turn might result in a hospital stay
- Unsure where to go: walk in clinic? Emergency?
- Seasonal flu et al

These factors don’t sit in neat boxes; they feed each other. Drag any node in the diagram below to see how a change ripples through the system. Notice the reinforcing loop on the left: admin burden burns doctors out, so fewer family doctors remain, which piles more admin on those still practising. That shortage pushes people into the ER, and the beds, our real bottleneck, stay full whether or not triage runs faster.

<Loopy
  data="[[[1,440,270,0.5,%22Family%2520Doctors%22,3],[2,200,410,0.5,%22Admin%2520Burden%22,1],[3,200,150,0.5,%22Doctor%2520Burnout%22,0],[4,660,150,0.5,%22ER%2520Visits%22,2],[5,880,300,0.5,%22Bed%2520Occupancy%22,0],[6,660,430,0.5,%22LTC%2520Waitlist%22,5]],[[2,3,40,1],[3,1,40,-1],[1,2,150,-1],[1,4,-40,-1],[4,5,-40,1],[6,5,40,1]],[[200,500,%22Reinforcing%2520loop%22],[880,190,%22The%2520bottleneck%22]],7%5D"
  title="Causal loop diagram: why faster ER triage doesn't empty full hospital beds"
/>

None of these problems will magically get fixed by AI. If we want our healthcare system to help us get well/stay well, look at the overall system.

One example of a hospital taking a systemic approach? Humber River Hospital has a command centre where they’re paying attention[^3] to:
- Emergency Department volume
- Bed allocations and assignments
- Room cleaning
- Critical care capacity
- Surgical scheduling
- Discharge planning

Reading the promotional PDF from GE[^4] the command centre is focused on getting the patients who need admission a bed faster and reducing pain, complications and secondary infections.

GE promotes this system as using AI. However, the AI isn’t the central feature. The value of this system is that people in the hospital are paying constant attention to how the hospital is working. If there is a constraint, they make changes to reduce the problem. The command centre is staffed by a cross disciplinary group of people, so that there is enough knowledge in the room to make good decisions.

AI is useful here, because they’ve studied the flow of the system. They’ve established useful metrics: getting people healthy and allowing them to leave hospital. Here’s the irony: the pattern-finding that actually helps predates ChatGPT and GenAI entirely. GE brands it “AI” but it’s not the AI the strategy is betting on.

The material available in public is promotional so the actual effectiveness of the real system is something I can’t see.

AI didn’t make Humber River Hospital more effective. Improving the flow in the system made it more effective. Predictive analytics is just a tool in this picture.

### Family Doctors and GenAI
Earlier we noted that the lack of family doctors is a contributing factor to over capacity.

After a full day of seeing patients, family doctors still have to write up charts documenting their findings, treatment and prescriptions. This is unpaid labour, the doctor is paid for the patient visit and the documentation is treated as overhead.

Family doctors are already dealing with burnout, it turns out that OHIP payments in many cases don’t cover the realistic costs of running a clinic (rental, front office staff, medical equipment, computers, etc.) In an attempt to reduce the unpaid labour, many doctors I know have turned to GenAI transcription tools. There are clearly documented problems with some of these tools making mistakes with both the diagnoses and medications[^5]. Yet the physicians I know report saving a considerable amount of time. Possibly another example of [GenAI making us feel more productive](/blog/using-genai-to-code-not-so-fast/) without making a big difference.

GenAI might help here, however we’ve solved a symptom. Family doctors are expected to run businesses (not their training) and are expected to handle a large number of administrative tasks along with seeing patients.

Transcription tools may help, but they don’t solve the underlying problem. The administrative burden on family doctors is a major factor in their burnout.

We need to fix the system, and not just the symptoms.

## Not a Magic Wand
GenAI isn’t a magic wand and it isn’t a panacea. In the right context, it can be very useful. Used in the wrong place, it can [make an organization more fragile, not more resilient](/blog/is-ai-making-your-organization-fragile-or-more-resilient/).

Humber River Hospital’s command centre is a good step in the right direction. If we want to make a meaningful difference in the healthcare system, we need to look wider than just an emergency room. In short, we want to understand why family doctors are leaving the profession. If we can’t keep them happy to stay in the profession, then we can’t expect to keep patients out of the emergency room. At the other end of the spectrum, since many hospital beds are occupied by patients waiting for long term care, we need to find compassionate ways to improve the long term care system. We may also need more hospital staff and more beds.

The Healthcare system in Canada is just one example of many. We have a productivity problem, but we can’t just tell people to use GenAI and expect an improvement. If we want to improve productivity, we need to look at each organization as a system, understand the bottlenecks in the system and focus on eliminating that bottleneck.

content.text:
Here are two LinkedIn drafts, both built from your own sentences in the post and both leaning into AI washing, just from different angles.

## Option A — Adoption isn't productivity (the target invites AI washing)

**Angle:** The policy-level critique. Uses the productivity-decline data and the strategy's own adoption target to define AI washing.

**Draft:**
> Canada has a real productivity problem, and we have for decades. In 1984, the Canadian economy was 88% as productive as the US per hour worked. By 2022, it had fallen to 71%.
>
> The new national AI strategy is an attempt to fix that. It promises a 3 percent increase in GDP from labour productivity, and aims to increase Canada's business adoption of AI from 12 percent today to 60 percent by 2034.
>
> Here's the problem: adoption of AI doesn't make an organization more productive. Dropping AI onto a broken process just automates the mess. A target like this invites AI washing: measure success by adoption rate, and organizations will claim they're "doing AI" to hit the number, whether or not anything meaningful changes.
>
> Saying a new technology will magically make us more productive doesn't make it so. If we want to improve productivity, we need to look at each organization as a system, understand the bottlenecks, and focus on eliminating them.
>
> What would you rather your organization be measured on: how much AI it adopted, or whether the work actually got easier?
>
> #AIinSoftwareDevelopment #Leadership

**Source lines:** "In 1984, the Canadian economy was 88% as productive... In 2022, it had fallen to 71%"; the 12%→60% adoption target; "A target like this invites AI washing..."; "Saying a new technology will magically make us more productive doesn't make it so."

They're intended to be a tool for the team to understand what is going on in their work and how it is progressing. A couple of Sprint Backlog anti-patterns are worth naming, because they're common and they're quiet.

When the Sprint Backlog is created during Sprint Planning, some teams decide who will work on which item. When all items are pre-assigned to team members, we have just planned for the first bottleneck.

The Sprint Backlog also loses its value when it's used for external purposes like reporting. When leadership uses it to look over the shoulders of the people doing the work, it often leads to overloading the Sprint Backlog with details that undermine and eliminate transparency. The Sprint Backlog is used only by the Scrum Team, and is not intended to be viewed by anyone else.
